title: Lecture 1: Course Introduction
subtitle: Course Introduction
text: Course Introduction Brain and behavior question → variables and hypotheses → mathematical model → simulation / analysis → data and estimation → testing and revision Explain computational neuroscience as a cycle of questions, data, models, and inference, rather than equating it with programming or the application of machine-learning algorithms. Distinguish descriptive, mechanistic, and normative models, and select an appropriate level of model for a given neuroscience question. Starting from a minimal input–output model, write testable predictions, residuals, and a parameter-estimation objective, and explain how each quantity is obtained experimentally. Organize the mathematical, programming, and neuroscience prerequisites into an actionable learning loop: know when to calculate, when to plot, and when to return to the biological hypothesis. This lecture presents computational neuroscience as a research strategy, not a particular software package, algorithm, or job title. The strategy may start from data and estimate neural representations, or start from a mechanistic hypothesis and build a model for simulation. Its essential standards are clear variables, computable predictions, falsifiable assumptions, and results that answer a neuroscience question. Later lectures apply this language to single neurons, population coding, vision, movement, decision-making, reinforcement learning, and memory. Equating computational neuroscience with “using computers” or “training neural networks.” Assuming that a good fit proves the proposed mechanism; different models can make similar predictions. Choosing a tool before defining the question, leaving variables, units, and falsifiable predictions unspecified. Treating firing rate as a directly observed continuous quantity even though it is usually a statistical estimate. Treating course logistics as permanent academic content; Here belongs to the 2025 course archive. This lecture establishes only the concepts and dependencies needed by the next 26 lectures; it is not a general survey of computational neuroscience. Minimal threshold-linear input–output model \(r(s) = [ws + b]\)+ Static, one-dimensional stimulus; nonnegative rate Generative model: distribution of the data given inputs and parameters \(P (y | x, \theta )\) Conditioning variables and random variables are defined explicitly Maximum-likelihood parameter estimate θb = arg \(\max P (y | x, \theta )\) \(\theta \) The model class and assumptions about data independence hold Prediction from a fitted model for a new input b yb = \(f (x; \theta )\) The relationship between the new input and the training distribution is stated Residual between observation and prediction error = y − yb Must have the same units as y computational neuroscience The study of computation in nervous systems using quantitative models, algorithms, and data analysis. model An explicit, simplified representation of variables, relationships, and assumptions. simulation Generation of state trajectories or synthetic data by applying a model's rules. inference Using data to constrain unknown states, parameters, or models. prediction A model's quantitative output for data not used in fitting, under specified conditions. falsifiability The property that some possible observation could conflict with a model's prediction. machine learning A family of methods that optimize predictive functions from data; it overlaps with computational neuroscience but is not identical to it. data science The broad practice of organizing, analyzing, computing with, and interpreting data. mechanistic model A model whose variables and interactions are interpreted as candidate biological processes. parameter A quantity held fixed during one model run but potentially estimated from data. Why is “this brain region activates during the task” not yet a mechanistic explanation? It reports only that activity and task co-occur. It does not specify the variables, connections, or dynamics that generate the activity, nor does it predict quantitatively how an intervention should change it. The instructor's background across neurobiology, physics, and applied mathematics reveals the field's working pattern. Experiments define the nervous-system objects and constraints. Mathematics compresses verbal hypotheses into relationships that can be derived. Computation extends those derivations beyond hand-calculable scales. Engineering forces models to produce operational outputs. These are not four unrelated labels; they form a chain from observation to explanation to test. A model fits its training set well but predicts new stimuli poorly. What does that tell you most directly? The model or estimation procedure has not captured a generalizable relationship. It may have too many degrees of freedom, inadequate training coverage, or omitted variables that change under the new stimuli. The model–data loop has five repeatable actions: define variables, write relationships, estimate parameters, predict held-out data, and inspect the error structure. In \(r(s)=\max(0,ws+b)\), s is stimulus intensity, r is mean firing rate, w controls slope, and b is the extrapolated intercept at zero stimulus. Data must constrain the parameters, and predictions must target observations that were not used for fitting. Why begin with a hand-calculable example before running a large simulation? It provides an independent expectation and quickly exposes errors in indices, signs, units, and boundary conditions. A smooth-looking large plot does not prove that an implementation matches its equations. Flipped learning requires exposure before class, but “I watched it” is not a completion criterion. A stronger standard is to perform four tasks without prompts: answer the guiding question in your own words, reconstruct one derivation, solve one numerical example, and identify at least one condition under which the model fails. If one step breaks, return to the corresponding section and repair it rather than replaying everything from the beginning. Which interpretation is supported by the schematic “Model–data feedback loop”? Fitting parameters is only the middle of the loop. A model must first predict data that were not used for fitting; systematic stimulus-dependent residuals then determine whether the hypothesis should be retained, revised, or replaced.

title: Lecture 2: Vectors, Matrices, and Probability
subtitle: Vectors, Matrices, and Probability
text: Vectors, Matrices, and Probability Objects and shapes → linear-algebra operations → probability distributions → joint / marginal / conditional distributions → Bayesian updating Determine the shape of each scalar, vector, or matrix before carrying out addition, inner products, outer products, matrix multiplication, or element-wise multiplication, and explain what the result represents. Use a determinant to decide whether a given two-by-two matrix is invertible, calculate its inverse by hand, and verify that the product is the identity matrix. From a probability mass function or density, calculate normalization, means, variances, marginals, and conditional distributions, and distinguish “uncorrelated” from “independent.” Derive Bayes' rule from the two factorizations of a joint probability and distinguish the prior, likelihood, evidence, and posterior clearly. This lecture establishes the grammar used by almost every later formula: first identify whether each object is a scalar, vector, or matrix and determine its shape; then decide whether the operation is defined. The probability material moves from univariate Bernoulli and exponential distributions to bivariate Gaussians, marginals, conditionals, and Bayes' rule. An expression that MATLAB can execute is not necessarily an operation defined in abstract mathematics, so program output must be interpreted separately from the meaning of its objects. Mistaking MATLAB scalar expansion for scalar+matrix addition in abstract linear algebra. Confusing * with.*: the former is matrix multiplication, whereas the latter is a Hadamard product. Calculating entries before checking shape and thereby assigning a result to an undefined operation. Treating a density value as the probability of one exact value of a continuous variable. Assuming that uncorrelated variables are always independent; this implication holds only in special cases such as a Gaussian distribution. Reversing the conditioning directions of posterior, likelihood, and prior. Interpreting clear all and inv in the MATLAB source literally as best practices. Numerical work generally favors solving a linear system over forming an explicit inverse. Keep MATLAB's scalar-plus-matrix behavior distinct from abstract linear algebra. Shape rule for matrix–vector multiplication Am×n \(xn\times 1 \to  ym\times 1\) The inner dimensions are equal Inner product uT \(v = u_{i} v i i\) The vectors have the same dimension Outer product uv T The output shape is len(u)×len(v) Euclidean norm \(\Vert w\Vert 2 = w_{\mathrm{T}} w A\) consistent row/column convention is used Variance identity \(\operatorname{Var}(X) = E[X 2 ] - E[X]2\) The second moment exists Definition of the CDF FX (x) = P (X ≤ x) Applies to both discrete and continuous variables Exponential PDF \(fX (x) = \lambda e^{-\lambda x} 1x\ge 0\) \(\lambda >0\) Bivariate Gaussian density 1 −1 (x−µ) e− 2 (x−µ) C 1 T \(p(x) = \sqrt  2\pi  \det C C\) is symmetric positive definite Bayes' rule \(P (B | A)P (A)\) \(P (A | B) = P (B)\) \(P(B)>0\) scalar A single number; it may be represented as a \(1\times 1\) object when the context is stated. vector An ordered set of components; this course uses column vectors by default. matrix A two-dimensional array organized by rows and columns that represents a linear map. inner product The sum of componentwise products of two vectors with the same dimension. outer product The matrix produced by multiplying a column vector by a row vector. Hadamard product Elementwise multiplication of objects with the same shape. singular matrix A square matrix that is not invertible and has determinant zero. probability mass function, PMF The probability assigned to each possible outcome of a discrete random variable. probability density function, PDF Probability density per unit interval for a continuous random variable. marginal distribution The distribution of one variable after summing or integrating over the others. conditional distribution A distribution renormalized after another event or variable is known. likelihood A function of model parameters that measures their relative support with the observations held fixed. prior A distribution over an unknown quantity before observing the current data. posterior The updated distribution obtained by combining likelihood and prior. Why can each output of A v be read as a weighted sum of one row of weights and the input? By definition, matrix multiplication gives \(y_{i}=\sum _j A_{ij} v_{j}\). Once output row i is fixed, the sum runs only over input index j, so that row lists how the output weights each input. Start with concrete objects: \(s=2\), \(u=(0,1)^{\mathrm{T}}\), \(v=(2,5)^{\mathrm{T}}\), \(w=(0,1,2,5)^{\mathrm{T}}\), and matrices A, B, and C. These are more than arithmetic exercises: a vector may represent responses from several neurons, and a matrix may represent a linear map from stimulus to response. Shape records the input and output slots. If you ignore it, you may swap neuron and condition indices even when the arithmetic itself is correct. Which distinct inputs does \(C=[[3,4],[6,8]]\) map to the same output, and how does that demonstrate noninvertibility? Because \(C(4,-3)^{\mathrm{T}}=(0,0)^{\mathrm{T}}\), any x and \(x+a(4,-3)^{\mathrm{T}}\) have the same output. The output cannot determine a, so it cannot recover a unique input. For a two-by-two matrix \(B=[[a,b],[c,d]]\), \(\det(B)=ad-bc\). Geometrically, the determinant is the signed area scale factor of the linear map. A zero determinant means that a two-dimensional region is compressed into a line or point, so distinct inputs yield the same output. Once the map flattens information, output alone cannot identify the original input and no inverse exists. This is the same fact as linear dependence among rows or columns. Why is \(P(D|\theta )\), viewed as a function of \(\theta\), called a likelihood but not equal to \(P(\theta |D)\)? The likelihood fixes the observed data and compares how well parameter values explain them. The parameter posterior must also incorporate a prior and normalize across every candidate parameter; the two expressions condition in opposite directions. A bivariate Gaussian is determined completely by its mean vector and covariance matrix. Integrating out one variable gives a Gaussian marginal; fixing an observation and renormalizing gives a Gaussian conditional distribution. Conditioning shifts the mean and reduces variance to the uncertainty left after accounting for the correlation. The derivation below gives the conditional mean, conditional variance, and Bayesian reweighting, allowing you to calculate the complete distribution rather than merely infer the tilt of an ellipse. Which interpretation is supported by the schematic “Conditioning a joint Gaussian shifts the mean and reduces the variance”? When two variables are correlated, fixing \(X_{2}\) takes a slice through the joint density. The conditional mean shifts along the correlation direction, while conditional variance decreases from \(\sigma _{1}^{2}\) to \(\sigma _{1}^{2}(1-c^{2})\). The curves are normalized illustrations of the formula, not empirical histograms.

title: Lecture 3: Differential Equations and Euler Simulation
subtitle: Differential Equations and Euler Simulation
text: Differential Equations and Euler Simulation State \(x(t)\)→ derivative / ODE → initial condition → analytic solution → Euler discretization → stability and error Translate the statement “the rate of change depends on the current state and input” into a first-order differential equation, and explain why an initial condition is part of a complete prediction. Derive the exact constant-input solution of \(\tau dx/dt=-x+I\) by hand and verify it using the initial value, long-time limit, and units. Derive the Euler update from the definition of a derivative, state the step-size condition for stability, and distinguish discrete numerical error from continuous-system behavior. Rewrite a second-order oscillator as two first-order equations, interpret its state-space trajectory, and audit the piecewise boundaries and indices in the supplied MATLAB code. A differential equation defines a full time trajectory through a local rate of change, while an initial condition selects one member of the solution family. An analytic solution exposes exact structure and enables limiting checks; Euler's method turns the derivative definition into an iterative update. A numerical result is trustworthy only when the step size is appropriate relative to the time constant, not merely because the code runs. Higher-order equations can be rewritten as coupled first-order systems by adding state variables, which is foundational for later network dynamics. Treating a derivative as the total change over a finite interval instead of the instantaneous rate obtained as \(\Delta t\to 0\). Dropping the initial condition or integration constant when solving by separation of variables. Assuming that executable code implies a sufficiently small \(\Delta t\). An Euler update evaluates \(I(t_{n})\), not the unknown \(I(t_{n+1})\); an off-by-one index changes the algorithm. Confusing the exact oscillatory dynamics with the outward spiral produced by explicit Euler. Confusing the time constant \(\tau\) with the simulation step \(\Delta t\). A code explanation must connect every MATLAB line to its differential equation, discrete update, and plotted result; potential bugs and incorrect source comments must be listed separately. First-order initial-value problem \(\dot{x} = f (x, t)\), \(x(0) = x_{0} f\) is regular enough to guarantee a solution Integral form of an ODE \(x(t) = x_{0} + f (x(t' ), t' )dt'\) 0 The integral follows the actual trajectory First-order system with constant input \(x(t) = I + (x_{0} - I)e^{-t/\tau } I\) is constant and \(\tau >0\) Explicit Euler method xn+1 = xn + ∆tf (xn, tn ) \(\Delta t\) is sufficiently small Euler stability interval for the decay equation 0 < ∆\(t/\tau  < 2\) Linear first-order test equation First-order form of the harmonic oscillator \(\dot{x} = y\), \(\dot{y} = -x\) Undamped, with unit angular frequency Conserved quantity of the exact oscillator, up to a constant factor \(E = x_{2} + y 2\) Exact continuous dynamics differential equation An equation that constrains an unknown function through its derivatives. initial condition A state specified at the starting time that selects one trajectory from a family of solutions. analytic solution An exact expression written in terms of known functions. numerical solution An approximation to the state at discrete time points. time constant The timescale over which a first-order exponential process removes about 63% of its initial gap. steady state A solution whose state no longer changes with time. Euler method Numerical integration by taking a small forward step along the current derivative. truncation error Local error caused by omitting higher-order Taylor terms in a finite-difference approximation. numerical stability Whether small perturbations decay during a discrete iteration instead of being amplified. coupled equations Equations in which the derivatives of multiple states depend on one another. phase space A space whose coordinates are all state variables and in which a trajectory is represented. If the input switches suddenly from \(I=5\) to \(I=-2\), which part of the solution changes? Does x jump instantly to −2? The new steady state is −2, and the value of x at the switching time becomes the new initial condition. A continuous first-order state does not jump; it approaches −2 exponentially with time constant \(\tau\). The examples \(dx/dt=x\) and \(d^{2}x/dt^{2}=-x\) show that a differential equation specifies a dynamical rule. A candidate solution is checked by substitution, not by visual resemblance. The derivative of \(x=e^t\) is \(e^t\), satisfying the first equation; the second derivative of \(x=\sin t\) is \(-\sin t\), satisfying the second. Initial conditions then select the amplitude and phase. Why does a discrete trajectory that alternates across steady state not immediately imply an oscillatory mechanism in the continuous system? This first-order continuous equation has only a real negative decay rate. Alternation may come from a negative Euler amplification factor. Reduce \(\Delta t\) and compare with the exact solution before calling it model dynamics rather than a numerical artifact. For \(\tau dx/dt=-x+I\), Euler gives \(x_{n+1}=x_{n}+(\Delta t/\tau )(-x_{n}+I)\). Define \(\alpha =\Delta t/\tau\) and \(y_{n}=x_{n}-I\) to obtain \(y_{n+1}=(1-\alpha )y_{n}\). The continuous deviation always decays smoothly; the discrete deviation is controlled by amplification factor \(a=1-\alpha\). Its magnitude shrinks only when \(|a|<1\). What two checks, at minimum, distinguish an outward spiral caused by the continuous model from one caused by the numerical method? First calculate a continuous invariant such as the energy derivative, or the system's eigenvalues. Then vary the step size and compare with an energy-preserving method or an exact solution. If continuous energy is constant while Euler energy grows, the artifact is localized. The accompanying code also simulates a first-order system with \(\tau =0.01 \mathrm{s}\), step 0.001 s, and duration 0.250 s. Inputs are 0, 2, 1, a cosine, and 0 in sequence. Each update reads the previous input \(I(t-1)\), as expected for the current-time slope in explicit Euler. The final condition is `time<0.250`, but the time vector includes the endpoint 0.250 exactly. Consequently, \(I(end)\) remains NaN and the last input point is not plotted normally. Which interpretation is supported by the schematic “Exact exponential decay versus Euler approximation”? For \(\tau dx/dt=-x\), forward Euler advances one step along the current tangent. With \(\Delta t=\tau /2\) it is stable, but at finite step size it decays faster than the exact exponential. Reducing \(\Delta t\) moves the discrete points toward the exact curve.

title: Lecture 4: Neurons I: Membrane Voltage, Circuits, and Integrate-and-Fire
subtitle: Neurons I: Membrane Voltage, Circuits, and Integrate-and-Fire
text: Neurons I: Membrane Voltage, Circuits, and Integrate-and-Fire Concentration gradient → electrochemical equilibrium → Nernst potential → membrane capacitance / channels → Kirchhoff's law → IF / LIF Build a consistent sign convention from the definitions of force, potential energy, electric potential, and membrane voltage, and explain how a concentration gradient and an electric field jointly determine net ionic flux. Derive the Nernst equation from the electrochemical equilibrium of a single ion, handling the valence z, the inside-to-outside concentration ratio, temperature, and voltage sign correctly. Map the lipid membrane, ion channels, and applied current onto a capacitor, conductance–battery branches, and a current source, then derive the membrane equation from charge conservation. Distinguish the perfect integrate-and-fire model from the leaky integrate-and-fire model, and calculate their slopes, time constants, steady-state voltages, rheobase currents, and first-spike times. State what the equivalent circuit, integrate-and-fire model, and action-potential mechanism each retain and omit, without interpreting model components as literal biological parts. The neural membrane is both a capacitor that separates charge and a conductance network formed by ion-selective channels. Diffusion drives ions down concentration gradients, while the electric field drives charged particles toward lower electric potential energy. Their balance defines each ion's reversal potential. The circuit equivalent is not a decorative analogy: it combines charge conservation, Ohm's law, and channel selectivity into a solvable equation for membrane voltage. Treating an equilibrium potential as the cell's actual instantaneous membrane voltage. Forgetting the sign convention V_m=inside−outside. Applying a cation's sign intuition to Cl−. Conflating current direction, positive-charge motion, and voltage change. Assuming that ions cross the membrane through the capacitor branch; an ideal capacitor represents redistribution of charge on the two sides of the membrane. Treating threshold and reset as an action potential generated naturally by the LIF differential equation. This lecture stops at the LIF equation. Do not fold in Lecture 5's full closed-form LIF solution or HH gating dynamics prematurely, though a clear preview at the end is useful. Membrane-voltage sign convention Vm = \(\varphi _{\mathrm{in}} - \varphi _{\mathrm{out}}\) Inside minus outside Nernst equilibrium potential kB \(T [c]_{\mathrm{out}}\) Ec = ln qc \([c]_{\mathrm{in}}\) Single-ion equilibrium at fixed temperature Definition of capacitance \(Q = CV C\) is approximately constant Capacitive current \(I = C \dot{V}\) \(Q=CV\) Leak current IL = GL (V − EL ) Linear passive conductance Subthreshold LIF equation C V̇ = Ie − GL (V − EL ) Threshold and reset are specified separately F-I slope of the pure IF model Ie \(r= C(VT - VR )\) Constant current, no refractory period, and no leak membrane voltage Electric potential inside the cell minus electric potential outside the cell. diffusion Net random motion driven by a concentration gradient. electric potential energy The energy \(q\phi\) of a charged particle in an electric potential. equilibrium potential The voltage at which the net flux of one ion is zero. reversal potential The voltage at which current through a channel changes direction; in the simplest case, it equals the equilibrium potential. conductance The reciprocal of resistance, \(G=1/R\). capacitance Charge stored per unit voltage, Q/V. Kirchhoff current law The algebraic sum of currents entering and leaving a node is zero. integrate-and-fire model An abstract model that integrates input, emits a spike at threshold, and resets. leaky integrator A state driven by input while exponentially relaxing toward a baseline. If \(\mathrm{Cl}^{-}\) had the same inside-to-outside concentration ratio, why would its equilibrium potential have the opposite sign from that of \(K^{+}\)? In the Nernst equation, signed valence z appears in the denominator. For \(\mathrm{Cl}^{-}\), \(z=-1\) reverses the sign of the logarithmic term, reflecting the reversal of electric force for a negative charge. The cell membrane separates two conducting saline solutions. Most of the fluid on either side remains nearly electroneutral: membrane voltage requires only a tiny fraction of ions to separate at the membrane surfaces, not a cell interior filled with negative charge. Use \(F=-\nabla U\) and \(\phi =U/q\), and define \(V_{m}=\phi _{\mathrm{in}}-\phi _{\mathrm{out}}\). A resting value near −60 mV means that the intracellular potential is lower. The same convention governs reversal potentials, channel currents, and action-potential diagrams. Why does increasing one channel conductance change both the steady-state voltage and the speed of approach? It gives that channel's reversal potential more weight in the steady-state average and increases \(G_{\mathrm{tot}}\), which reduces the membrane time constant \(C/G_{\mathrm{tot}}\); voltage therefore approaches the new steady state faster. For fixed C, \(Q=CV\) means that changing voltage requires changing surface charge. Differentiating gives \(dQ/dt=C dV/dt\), and the definition \(I=dQ/dt\) therefore gives \(I_{C}=C dV/dt\). Injecting 100 pA into a 200 pF capacitor produces a slope of 0.5 mV/ms. A capacitor alone does not set a steady state: as long as a nonzero constant net current persists, voltage continues to change linearly. Why does 100 pA eventually produce a spike in perfect IF but never produce one in the LIF model above? Perfect IF has no opposing leak, so positive current continues to charge the capacitor. In LIF, leak grows during depolarization until it exactly balances 100 pA at −55 mV, a steady state below the −50 mV threshold. Adding a leak branch gives \(C dV/dt=I_{e}-G_{L}(V-E_{L})\). Leak grows with the displacement of V from \(E_{L}\) and always pulls voltage toward \(E_{L}\). With \(\tau _{m}=C/G_{L}\) and \(V_{\mathrm{inf}}=E_{L}+I_{e}/G_{L}\), the equation becomes \(\tau _{m} dV/dt=-V+V_{\mathrm{inf}}\). Under constant input, \(V(t)=V_{\mathrm{inf}}+(V_{0}-V_{\mathrm{inf}})e^{-t/\tau _{m}}\); voltage approaches a finite steady state exponentially instead of rising without bound. Which interpretation is supported by the schematic “Current conservation in the membrane equivalent circuit”? Node conservation divides the applied current into two parts: C \(dV_{m}/dt\) changes the charge stored across the membrane, while \(\sum G_{x}(V_{m}-E_{x})\) flows through ionic branches. \(E_{x}\) sets the zero-current voltage of a branch, and \(G_{x}\) sets how strongly that branch pulls \(V_{m}\) toward \(E_{x}\).

title: Lecture 5: Neurons II: LIF Solution and Hodgkin–Huxley
subtitle: Neurons II: LIF Solution and Hodgkin–Huxley
text: Neurons II: LIF Solution and Hodgkin–Huxley LIF ODE → steady state → threshold time → exact F-I relation → HH conductances → gating / refractory period Rewrite the LIF equation in time-constant–steady-state form and explain the exponential trajectory after a current step begins and ends. Derive the exact interspike interval and F–I curve of the LIF model from the threshold condition, and analyze behavior near rheobase and in the strong-input limit. Interpret current direction and maximal conductance in the leak, \(\mathrm{Na}^{+}\), and \(K^{+}\) branches of the Hodgkin–Huxley membrane equation. Derive a gating variable's steady state and time constant from the transition rates of a two-state channel, and explain activation, inactivation, and refractoriness. Explain how area normalization, multicompartment propagation, and cellular diversity extend a point-neuron model without confusing passive subthreshold decay with active action-potential regeneration. An LIF model treats each spike as a threshold-and-reset event, so its threshold-crossing time and firing rate can be derived analytically. The HH model instead explains the spike waveform through feedback among dynamic Na/K conductances. The two models answer different questions: LIF provides a tractable abstraction for networks and coding, whereas HH addresses ionic mechanisms and waveform shape. Membrane time constant, interspike interval, and refractory period must remain distinct. Confusing \(\tau _{m}\), the ISI, and refractory interval \(\delta\). Assuming that \(V_{\infty }=V_{T}\) leads to a threshold crossing in finite time; the voltage only approaches threshold asymptotically. Treating the threshold-linear F-I relation as the exact LIF result. Treating m, h, and n as numbers of ion channels. Forgetting that current=conductance×driving force; increasing a gate does not by itself determine current direction. Treating HH as the unique model of every neuron. Keep membrane time constant, interspike interval, and refractory period separate. Likewise distinguish channel activation probability, conductance, and ionic current. Membrane time constant \(\tau m = C/GL\) Passive linear membrane Steady-state voltage under constant current \(V_{\infty } = E_{L} + I/GL I\) is constant LIF rheobase IT = GL (VT − EL ) \(V_{R}\) does not affect the steady-state crossing criterion Time from reset to threshold \(V_{\infty } - VR\) ∆\(t = \tau m \ln V \infty  - VT\) \(V_{\infty }>V_{T}\) Firing rate with a refractory period r = 1/(δ + ∆t) Periodic response to constant current Conductance-based ionic current \(I_{\mathrm{ion}} = \bar{G}\) popen \((V - E_{\mathrm{rev}} )\) The sign convention and driving force are explicit Two-state gate kinetics \(\dot{n} = \alpha n (1 - n) - \beta n n\) \(0\le n\le 1\) membrane time constant The timescale \(C/G_{L}\) of a passive membrane's exponential response. steady-state voltage The value \(V_{\infty }\) at which the derivative vanishes under constant input. threshold current / rheobase The smallest indefinitely sustained constant current that can elicit a spike. interspike interval, ISI The elapsed time between adjacent spikes. absolute refractory period The minimum interval after a spike during which another spike cannot occur. maximal conductance The conductance scale when all relevant channels are open. activation A gating process in which depolarization increases channel opening. inactivation A process in which sustained depolarization reduces channel availability. cable equation An equation describing how voltage propagates and attenuates through space along a neurite. multicompartment model A representation that discretizes morphology into electrically coupled compartments. If C and \(G_{L}\) both double, how do \(V_{\mathrm{inf}}\) and \(\tau _{m}\) change? \(\tau _{m}=C/G_{L}\) remains unchanged. For the same total current \(I_{e}\), \(I_{e}/G_{L}\) is halved, so \(V_{\mathrm{inf}}\) moves closer to \(E_{L}\). If input also doubles in proportion to area, the steady-state offset can remain unchanged. The first two pages rebuild the circuit from an ideal capacitor to a leaky integrate-and-fire membrane. An ideal capacitor obeys \(C dV/dt=I_{e}\) and has no steady state under constant current. Adding leak gives \(C dV/dt=I_{e}-G_{L}(V-E_{L})\). Above \(E_{L}\), outward leak current is positive and opposes further depolarization; below \(E_{L}\), current reverses and drives voltage upward. Thus \(E_{L}\) is the stable point with no input. Why can a complex or negative time returned by the crossing formula when \(I_{e}<I_{T}\) not be interpreted as an unusual form of spiking? The derivation assumes \(V_{\mathrm{inf}}>V_{T}\), making the logarithmic ratio a positive number greater than 1. At a subthreshold steady state, the trajectory never crosses threshold; an expression outside its domain simply signals that the assumption failed. Set \(V(t)=V_{\mathrm{inf}}+(V_{R}-V_{\mathrm{inf}})e^{-t/\tau _{m}}\) equal to \(V_{T}\) to obtain period \(\Delta t=\tau _{m} \ln[(V_{\mathrm{inf}}-V_{R})/(V_{\mathrm{inf}}-V_{T})]\) and frequency \(f=1/\Delta t\). This relation is not linear. As \(I_{e}\) approaches \(I_{T}\), the denominator voltage difference approaches zero and \(\Delta t\) diverges. At larger \(I_{e}\), the period shortens and approaches the linear strong-input approximation of a perfect integrator. If \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) both double, why does \(n_{\mathrm{inf}}\) remain fixed while \(\tau _{n}\) is halved? Steady state depends only on the ratio \(\alpha /(\alpha +\beta )\), so the common factor cancels. The time constant is the reciprocal of total transition rate; doubling both rates halves the relaxation time. During the action-potential upstroke, rapid growth of Na activation m produces inward Na current and positive feedback. Na inactivation h falls with depolarization while K activation n rises more slowly; together they terminate the upstroke and repolarize the membrane. After a spike, h has not recovered and n remains elevated, making another depolarization difficult. This is the kinetic origin of refractoriness. It differs from the fixed \(\delta\) imposed in LIF, although \(\delta\) can approximate its rate-limiting effect. Which interpretation is supported by the schematic “Threshold and refractoriness jointly shape the LIF F–I curve”? When \(I_{e}\le I_{T}\), the subthreshold steady state cannot reach threshold, so firing rate is zero. Above \(I_{T}\), the logarithmic term in the threshold-crossing time shapes the curve, while the absolute refractory period \(\delta\) limits the strong-input rate to \(1/\delta\).

title: Lecture 6: Neural Coding I: Poisson Spikes and Maximum Likelihood
subtitle: Neural Coding I: Poisson Spikes and Maximum Likelihood
text: Neural Coding I: Poisson Spikes and Maximum Likelihood Stimulus / task → voltage → spikes → raster / PSTH → Poisson variability → encoding \(P(n|s) \to MLE\)/ Fisher information Explain how the analysis moves from the mechanisms that generate action potentials to observable spike sequences, and identify which single-cell details are retained or averaged away in a coding analysis. Interpret the stimulus, MT recording, spike train, raster, and PSTH in a random-dot motion experiment, and calculate firing rates by hand from raw counts. Use the Fano factor and the coefficient of variation of interspike intervals to distinguish count variability from interval variability, and state the statistical object measured by each. Derive the window-count and waiting-time distributions of a homogeneous Poisson process, and explain how a constantly driven LIF neuron differs from Poisson spiking. Write the likelihood, log-likelihood, maximum-likelihood estimate, and Fisher information for a population of independent Poisson neurons, and relate likelihood curvature to estimation uncertainty. Neural encoding requires more than drawing a tuning curve: it specifies the full response distribution conditional on the stimulus. A Poisson model jointly predicts count variance≈mean, exponential ISIs, and independent increments. These are testable assumptions, not universal facts. A population likelihood multiplies the evidence from neurons; the log-likelihood turns that product into a sum, and its curvature connects decoding precision to Fisher information. Treating firing rate as a continuous signal measured directly by the electrode. Treating a raster, a count, a PSTH, and a rate as the same object. Concluding that a spike train is fully Poisson merely because \(\mathrm{Fano}\approx 1\). Ignoring observation window T and thereby confusing the units of rate and count. Reversing \(P(n|s)\) and \(P(s|n)\). Assuming independence in a population likelihood without stating it. Firing rate is not a directly observed continuous signal; it is generally a statistical model quantity or estimate. Neuropixels and head-direction-cell data are useful transfer examples, while MT remains the original example. Expected count in an observation window \(\lambda  = rT\) Homogeneous rate Poisson PMF \(P (K = k) = \lambda _{k} e^{-\lambda } /k\)! Independent increments Fano factor \(F = \operatorname{Var}(K)/E[K]\) Counts across trials under the same condition Poisson ISI density fISI \((t) = re^{-rt}\) Constant rate ISI irregularity CV = SD(ISI)/E[ISI] \(\operatorname{Mean}>0\) Independent-population likelihood \(Y P (k | \theta ) = P (k_{i} | \theta )\) i Conditional independence Maximum-likelihood decoder θb = arg \(\max \ell (\theta )\) A specified encoding model Fisher information \(J = -E[\ell '' (\theta )]\) A regular differentiable model neural encoding A mapping from a stimulus or state to a response distribution. spike train A sequence of discrete spike times. raster plot A visualization of spike times arranged by trial. peri-stimulus time histogram, PSTH An average spike-rate estimate obtained by binning across trials. Fano factor Count variance divided by count mean. point process A probability model for random event times. independent increments Independence of event counts in nonoverlapping time intervals. tuning curve Expected response as a function of a stimulus parameter. likelihood Support for a stimulus or parameter after the response is observed. maximum-likelihood estimate, MLE The parameter or stimulus estimate that maximizes the likelihood. Fisher information Local sensitivity of a probability distribution to a small parameter change. Why does an accurate count model not establish that precise spike timing contains no additional information? It establishes only that counts suffice for the chosen task. To determine whether timing adds predictive information beyond counts, compare the count model with a model that retains timing on independent data. Na activation, Na inactivation, K activation, and the refractory period constrain observable spike sequences: the absolute refractory period imposes a lower bound on adjacent interspike intervals, recovery of gating variables introduces history dependence, and conductances and morphology shape the stimulus-to-spike transformation. Thus, even a coding model that uses only counts cannot permit unbounded firing rates or negative counts. Compressed mechanisms remain present as boundary conditions on the statistical description. Why can concatenating all trials into one long spike train before making a histogram conceal important structure? Concatenation discards alignment to each stimulus onset and the identity of each trial. It can no longer separate time-locked changes in the mean, trial-to-trial count variability, and slow state drift, and it may create artificial intervals at concatenation boundaries. Each row of a raster represents one trial, each tick represents one spike, and the horizontal axis is time relative to stimulus onset. A raster displays both mean temporal structure and trial differences. If many rows become denser around 100 ms after stimulus onset, the conditional rate has increased during that period; variation in event counts and times across rows shows that repeated responses are not deterministic trajectories. A raster is not a rate curve: visual density must be converted to a normalized count before experiments can be compared. Why does taking the logarithm of a product of likelihood terms leave the location of the maximum-likelihood estimate unchanged? The natural logarithm is strictly increasing on positive numbers, so it preserves the ordering of candidate likelihoods. Taking logs only changes products into sums and improves numerical stability; it does not change the maximizer. If neurons are conditionally independent given \(\theta\), the population likelihood is a product of neuron-wise terms. Its log-likelihood is ℓ(θ)=Σ_i[N_i ln(f_i(θ)T)−f_i(θ)T−ln(N_i!)]. The maximum-likelihood estimate \(\theta _{\mathrm{hat}}\) is the direction under which the observed counts are most probable. Factorial terms that do not depend on \(\theta\) may be omitted when finding the maximum, but they still matter when calculating normalized probabilities or comparing different datasets. Which interpretation is supported by the schematic “Information-compression chain from voltage traces to a PSTH”? Threshold detection first compresses a continuous trace into event times. The raster retains each trial's event structure, whereas the PSTH divides the total spike count in a time bin by \(K\Delta t\), yielding a rate averaged across trials while discarding trial identity.

title: Lecture 7: Neural Coding II: Population Decoding, Fisher Information, and Bayes
subtitle: Neural Coding II: Population Decoding, Fisher Information, and Bayes
text: Neural Coding II: Population Decoding, Fisher Information, and Bayes Population likelihood → Fisher information → CRLB → noise covariance → information limitation → bias–variance tradeoff Explain how a population with diverse preferred directions resolves ambiguities in single-neuron tuning, and write the population Poisson likelihood. Derive Fisher information from the population log-likelihood, distinguishing the contributions of neuron count N, observation time T, and tuning-curve shape. State the assumptions of the Cramér–Rao lower bound and relate perceptual error to neural decoding precision without treating the bound as achieved performance. Calculate the variance of pooled correlated counts, use the inverse covariance matrix to explain harmful noise along the signal direction, and distinguish the existence of correlation from a limitation on information. Derive the bias–variance decomposition and explain how biased or Bayesian decoders can trade prior-induced bias for reduced variance. A single tuning curve often gives similar rates for multiple stimuli, but a population response pattern can resolve the ambiguity. Under ideal assumptions of independent Poisson neurons and uniformly distributed preferred directions, Fisher information grows linearly with N and T. Noise correlations, decoder mismatch, and behavioral constraints can make real-population performance saturate. A Bayesian prior trades a controlled bias for reduced variance. Treating the CRLB as the observed error of every decoder instead of a conditional lower bound. Assuming that positive correlation is always harmful and negative correlation is always beneficial. Conflating three levels: the encoding distribution, the decoding algorithm, and behavior. Automatically attributing saturation of Fisher information to one biological mechanism. Ignoring the modified bound for a biased decoder. Treating a prior as extra data instead of an assumption about stimulus frequency or structure. Keep three levels explicit: the neural encoding distribution, the decoder algorithm, and behavioral performance. The existence of correlation does not establish whether a particular decoder uses or ignores it. Fisher information of an independent Poisson population \(X J =T (f_{i}' )2 /f_{i} i\) Counts are independent Unbiased \(CRLB \operatorname{Var}(\hat{\theta }) \ge  1/J\) Regularity and unbiasedness Noise covariance \(C_{ij} = \operatorname{Cov}(r_{i}, r_{j} )\) Residuals across trials at a fixed stimulus Pearson noise correlation \(\rho i_{j} = C_{ij} /(\sigma _{i} \sigma _{j} )\) Nonzero variances Mahalanobis separation d2M = ∆µT C −1 ∆µ C is positive definite Bias–variance decomposition M \(SE = \operatorname{Var} +b_{2}\) Scalar estimator Bayesian decoding \(P (s|n) \propto  P (n|s)P (s)\) The posterior is properly normalized population code The joint response pattern of multiple neurons. Cramér-Rao lower bound An information-theoretic lower bound on the variance of an unbiased estimator under regularity conditions. noise correlation Correlation of trial residuals at a fixed stimulus. signal correlation Similarity of tuning curves across stimuli. covariance matrix A matrix containing the variance of each dimension and every pairwise covariance. Mahalanobis distance Distance normalized by the noise covariance. information-limiting correlation Shared noise along the stimulus-signal direction that cannot be removed by averaging a larger population. suboptimal decoder A readout that does not use all information available in the encoding distribution. bias The difference between an estimator's mean and the true value. regularization A constraint or prior used to reduce variance or complexity. Why need a high firing rate at the peak of a tuning curve not contribute the greatest local Fisher information? The Poisson information term is \((f')^{2}/f\). Although f is large at the peak, the slope f' is generally zero, so the mean barely changes under an infinitesimal stimulus change and local information may be zero. A single bell-shaped tuning curve can give the same firing rate on either side of its peak, so count \(k_{i}\) may have equal likelihood under directions \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\). Neuron i in a population has preferred direction \(\theta _{i}\) and tuning \(f_{i}(\theta )=f(\theta -\theta _{i})\). Although the two stimuli are degenerate for one neuron, they produce different count patterns across other neurons. The joint probability compares the entire pattern, allowing distributed preferences to resolve a single neuron's ambiguity. Why does saturation of performance in a simple left-versus-right pooling model not prove that the Fisher information of the full neural population saturates? Simple pooling uses only one projection of response space and may discard other decodable directions. To determine whether the population itself is information-limited, analyze the full covariance and mean derivative or compare stronger decoders. First distinguish two kinds of “correlation.” Signal correlation compares conditional means or tuning shapes across stimuli. Noise correlation fixes the stimulus and compares trial-wise deviations from each neuron's conditional mean. Only the latter enters the present pooling variance. Suppose the \(N_{R}\) residuals in a right-choice pool each have variance \(\sigma _{R}^{2}\) and every distinct pair has correlation \(c_{R}\). The variance of the pool average R is \(c_{R}\sigma _{R}^{2}+(1-c_{R})\sigma _{R}^{2}/N_{R}\). The independent component disappears as \(N_{R}\) grows, but the shared residual remains. Why does a reasonable Bayesian posterior usually depend less on the prior when data are highly reliable? Reliable data produce a sharp likelihood whose relative variation in the posterior product greatly exceeds that of a smooth prior. After normalization, probability concentrates near the likelihood peak, and the prior makes only a small correction. The biased Cramér–Rao bound is \(\operatorname{Var}(\hat{s})\ge [1+b'(s)]^{2}/J(s)\). If the estimator's mean response changes more slowly than the true stimulus, b' is negative and the variance bound may lie below the unbiased value 1/J; squared bias is the price. This bound still requires regularity conditions and is not a prescription for choosing a bias function. Compare full MSE or a task-relevant loss. Which interpretation is supported by the schematic “Fisher information in an independent Poisson population scales with NT”? For uniform tuning and conditional independence, \(J\approx NTj_{f}\). Thus, with tuning shape fixed, doubling either neuron count N or observation time T doubles information, whereas asymptotic error standard deviation shrinks only as \(1/\sqrt{NT}\).

title: Lecture 8: Neural Networks I: Spikes, Convolution, and E/I Balance
subtitle: Neural Networks I: Spikes, Convolution, and E/I Balance
text: Neural Networks I: Spikes, Convolution, and E/I Balance Spike-train δ-sum → kernel / convolution → coupled network → \(\operatorname{Poisson} E/I\) input → mean versus variance → failure of 1/N scaling Interpret the direction and shape of recurrent weights \(W_{ij}\) and input weights \(U_{ij}\), and explain their roles in coupled membrane equations. Represent a spike train as a sum of Dirac \(\delta\) functions, then use convolution to turn discrete spikes into synaptic input with a time course. Calculate the mean and variance of the total charge delivered by independent excitatory and inhibitory Poisson inputs within a finite time window. Compare the large-network scalings \(W\sim 1/N\) and \(W\sim 1/\sqrt N\), explaining why the former suppresses fluctuations and why the latter requires strong E/I cancellation. Distinguish excitation-dominated, inhibition-dominated, and balanced fluctuation-driven firing from voltage trajectories, and explain why dynamic balance does not mean that the current is exactly zero at every instant. The Dirac delta makes each spike time an integrable event, and convolution of a synaptic kernel with a spike train produces a continuous current. In the large-N limit, a proposed weight scaling must be checked for both mean and variance. Scaling as 1/N keeps the mean finite but suppresses fluctuations to zero. Balanced \(1/\sqrt N\) scaling lets large excitation and inhibition cancel in the mean while preserving \(O(1)\) fluctuations. Treating \(\delta (t)\) as an ordinary infinite number at \(t=0\). Reversing the time direction of \(K(t-t')\) and \(K(t')\) in a convolution. Forgetting to square the weight when calculating variance. Forgetting that inhibition contributes negatively to the mean but positively to the variance. Checking only mean scaling and not variance scaling. Interpreting E/I balance as exact equality of excitation and inhibition at every instant. The scaling derivations in this lecture are easy to distort by skipping steps. Calculate mean and variance separately and state the independence assumption explicitly. Distributional representation of a spike train ∆\((t) = \delta (t - t_{k} )\) k Defined through integration Synaptic filtering (K ∗ ∆)\((t) = K(t - t' )\)∆\((t' )dt'\) For causal K, depends only on the past Variance of an independent sum ∑ ∑ Var( a i Xi ) = a2i \(\operatorname{Var}(X_{i} )\) The \(X_{i}\) are independent Weak mean-field weights \(W \sim  1/N\) \(\mathrm{Variance}\to 0\) under independence Balanced-network scaling \(W \sim  1/ N E/I\) cancellation is required Balanced net \(\operatorname{mean} E[QE + QI ] = O(1)\) Large signed currents cancel Dirac delta A generalized function, or distribution, that samples a function under integration. convolution An operation that shifts a kernel across the input history, weights it, and sums the result. synaptic kernel The time-dependent response caused by one presynaptic spike. recurrent weight The connection strength from neuron \(j\to i\) within a network. input weight The connection from an external input neuron→recurrent-network neuron. excitation-inhibition balance A state in which large excitatory and inhibitory currents approximately cancel in their means. dynamic balance Balance generated online by recurrent feedback rather than imposed as moment-by-moment equality. order of magnitude The leading scaling as N grows, such as \(O(1)\) or \(O(\sqrt N)\). irregular spiking Spike timing with highly variable ISIs that is approximately Poisson-like. Why should \(\delta (t_{k})\) not be treated as an infinite number that must be stored directly in code? \(\delta\) is defined by how it acts under integration. Numerical implementations usually store event indices and add a discrete kernel afterward, or approximate the event with area 1 in a finite bin. Storing infinity directly would break units and arithmetic. The network contains N interconnected neurons and M external inputs. \(W_{ij}\) is the recurrent weight \(j\to i\), and \(U_{ij}\) is the weight from external input j→network neuron i. For each i, the membrane equation contains leak, every network sender, and every external sender. Whether diagonal entries of W allow self-connections is a modeling choice. A network is recurrent when W contains feedback paths, not because of where nodes happen to be drawn. Why does inhibition enter the mean with a negative sign but still enter the independent variance with a positive sign? Variance measures squared deviations from the mean. Multiplication by −W only reverses the direction of a fluctuation; its squared magnitude remains \(W^{2}\), so independent uncertainty from both excitation and inhibition increases total variance. Using \(E[K]=\operatorname{Var}(K)=r\Delta t\) gives \(E[Q]=(N_{\mathrm{EW},Er,E}-N_{\mathrm{IW},Ir,I})\Delta t\). Independence gives \(\operatorname{Var}(Q)=(N_{\mathrm{EW},E}^{2}r_{E}+N_{\mathrm{IW},I}^{2}r_{I})\Delta t\). E/I contributions can cancel in the mean, but their variances cannot cancel merely because their signs differ. If inputs are correlated, pairwise covariance terms must be added and the independent formula may underestimate or otherwise alter the fluctuations. Why is a net input mean near zero insufficient evidence that the network is in a strongly balanced state? Weak inputs can also give zero net mean. Strong balance additionally requires large separate E and I means that cancel at leading order, finite net variance, and the predicted scaling as connectivity changes. The balance condition is sensitive to relative mismatch. Each canceled term is \(O(\sqrt N)\), so if their relative mismatch remains constant, the net input also grows as \(\sqrt N\). Through \(E\to I\), \(I\to E\), recurrent connections, and external drive, network dynamics must adjust firing rates so that mean inhibition tracks mean excitation. Dynamic balance is a network-generated state, not merely a manual choice of equal external rates. Which interpretation is supported by the schematic “A strongly coupled network retains finite fluctuations after balance”? Under \(W\sim 1/\sqrt N\), the conditional means of excitatory and inhibitory input are each \(O(\sqrt N)\) and must cancel at leading order. Their instantaneous difference remains \(O(1)\), so net input is not zero at every instant and can continue to drive irregular spiking.

title: Lecture 9: Neural Networks II: Synaptic Dynamics and Rate Models
subtitle: Neural Networks II: Synaptic Dynamics and Rate Models
text: Neural Networks II: Synaptic Dynamics and Rate Models Integrating factor → causal exponential kernel → synaptic-current ODE → spike averaging → F-I nonlinearity → rate dynamics Use an integrating factor to derive the causal solution of \(\tau dx/dt=-x+I(t)\), and recognize it as the convolution of the input with an exponential kernel. Explain the area, time constant, and causality of a normalized exponential kernel, and calculate its response to a step or impulse input. Rewrite convolution with an exponential synapse as a first-order synaptic-current ODE, and count the 2N continuous states and discrete events in a network of N neurons. Approximate spike trains by firing rates through Poisson averaging, and distinguish the dynamical assumptions and relevant timescales of three rate models. Write the feedforward layer \(h^{(\ell )}=F(U^{(\ell )}h^{(\ell -1)})\), check weight shapes, and explain why nonlinearity prevents a multilayer composition from collapsing to one linear map. The solution of a first-order linear ODE is the causal exponential convolution of its past input; conversely, exponential convolution can be implemented by an ODE with one additional state variable. This equivalence turns a spiking network into a coupled voltage-and-current system and, under temporal averaging and timescale separation, produces rate models. Different rate-model forms make different assumptions about which variables are fast or slow and cannot be interchanged merely because they look similar. Omitting the \(1/\tau\) normalization of the exponential kernel. Conflating membrane \(\tau\), synaptic \(\tau _{s}\), and rate-response \(\tau _{r}\). Automatically equating a statistical firing-rate estimate with a dynamical rate variable. Making a fast-variable approximation without writing the derivative that is set to zero. Ignoring the biological problem of negative rates when using a tanh or linear F-I function. Conflating feedforward architecture with backpropagation training. Distinguish a statistical description of spike rate from a dynamical firing-rate variable. They are related, but they are not automatically the same object. Causal exponential kernel \(K\tau  (t) = e^{-t/\tau } H(t)/\tau \) \(\tau >0\) Linear low-pass solution \(x = K\tau  \ast  I\) The transient has been handled Exponential-synapse ODE \(\tau s\) I˙ = \(-I + u(t)\) Single-exponential kernel Instantaneous F-I approximation \(h = F(I)\) Rate response is fast Dynamic rate response \(\tau r\) \(\dot{h} = -h + F(I)\) Smooth population rate Feedforward layer h(ℓ) = F(W (ℓ) h(ℓ−1) ) Shape-compatible weights integrating factor A function that turns the left side of a first-order linear ODE into a product derivative. causal kernel A filter that is zero at negative times and depends only on past input. synaptic time constant The timescale of synaptic-current integration or decay. firing-rate response time The timescale on which a population rate approaches \(F(I)\). time-scale separation A regime in which one variable is much faster than another and can be approximately eliminated. F-I function A nonlinearity mapping input current to steady firing rate. threshold-linear Zero below threshold and increasing linearly above threshold. \(\operatorname{sigmoid} A\) smooth S-shaped function with lower and upper saturation. feedforward network An architecture in which information moves in one direction across layers without a recurrent loop. If the kernel is incorrectly written \(e^{-t/\tau }H(t)\), omitting \(1/\tau\), what happens to the long-run response to a constant input? If the weight units from this lecture's area-normalized convention are retained, the kernel area changes from 1 to \(\tau\) and the steady-state response becomes \(\tau I_{0}\). If peak normalization is intentional, weights must instead be interpreted as amplitudes and their units checked again. Consider \(\tau dx/dt=-x+I(t)\). Moving terms and dividing by \(\tau\) gives \(dx/dt+x/\tau =I(t)/\tau\). After multiplication by \(e^{t/\tau }\), the left side becomes \(d[xe^{t/\tau }]/dt\) by the product rule. Integrating from initial time \(t_{0}\) to the present t retains both an initial-condition term and a forced integral. If the system is assumed to have been stable since the distant past and the initial transient has vanished, the lower limit can instead be written as \(-\infty\). Why is an event-driven implementation less sensitive to dt than approximating \(\delta\) as a single bin of fixed height? An event-driven implementation applies the jump derived by integration and preserves impulse area. Unless fixed height is scaled by 1/dt, changing the time step changes both the area and total input. For network neuron i, the input events are \(S_{i}(t)=\sum _jW_{ij}\Delta _{j}(t)+\sum _jU_{ij}X_{j}(t)\). The synaptic state therefore obeys \(\tau _{s} dI_{i}/dt=-I_{i}+S_{i}(t)\), while the membrane state obeys C \(dV_{i}/dt=-G_{L}(V_{i}-E_{L})+I_{i}\). Each i has two continuous variables, \(V_{i}\) and \(I_{i}\), so N neurons have 2N ODE states in total. Why is \(\tau _{s}\ll \tau _{h} a\) mathematical justification for deleting the synaptic derivative, whereas “the model should be simpler” is not? The timescale ratio supplies a testable small parameter and an expected error: the fast variable relaxes before the slow variable changes. Without timescale separation, deleting the derivative changes delay, stability, and transients and must be tested against data. The first approximation assumes that the rate responds rapidly, sets \(h=F(I)\) directly, and retains only synaptic dynamics. A more complete second model adds \(\tau _{h} dh/dt=-h+F(I)\), keeping separate response times for I and h. If synapses are much faster than rate, \(\tau _{s}\ll \tau _{h}\), set \(I\approx Wh+Ux\) to obtain the common form \(\tau _{h} dh/dt=-h+F(Wh+Ux)\). Every deleted derivative must be justified by an explicit timescale separation. Which interpretation is supported by the schematic “The synaptic time constant determines how long one spike is retained”? For a peak-normalized exponential response, larger \(\tau _{s}\) makes the effect of a spike decay more slowly and preserves a longer memory. Under the area-normalized kernel \(K_{s}=\tau _{s}^{-1}e^{-t/\tau _{s}}\), the peak also changes as \(1/\tau _{s}\), so the normalization convention must be checked before curves are compared.

title: Lecture 10: Synaptic Plasticity
subtitle: Synaptic Plasticity
text: Synaptic Plasticity \(LTP/LTD/STDP \to NMDA-\mathrm{Ca}^{2+}\)→ Hebbian/covariance rule → covariance eigenmodes → positive feedback → Oja/BCM stabilization Connect Hebb's hypothesis, LTP/LTD, the STDP timing window, and the NMDA–Ca2+–AMPA mechanism into a conditional explanatory sequence, distinguishing empirical regularities from proposed mechanisms. Derive the expected weight dynamics \(E[dw/dt]=Cw\) from a centered firing-rate Hebbian rule, explaining vector orientation, matrix shape, and why mean subtraction permits depression. Use a quadratic form to prove that a covariance matrix is symmetric and positive semidefinite, then use an eigenbasis to explain why the direction of greatest variance grows fastest. Compare how synaptic scaling, Oja's rule, and the BCM sliding threshold regulate overall magnitude, local normalization, and the boundary between LTP and LTD. Distinguish unsupervised, supervised, and reward-based learning, and explain how an error, reward, or reward-prediction error can gate plasticity as a third factor. This lecture joins three levels of synaptic plasticity: experimental phenomena (LTP/LTD/STDP), proposed molecular mechanisms (NMDA-dependent \(\mathrm{Ca}^{2+}\) signaling and AMPA trafficking), and abstract learning rules. A basic Hebbian rule amplifies high-variance eigenmodes of input covariance but also creates positive feedback and unbounded growth. Synaptic scaling, Oja's rule, and BCM stabilize the system through global normalization, local weight-dependent decay, and a dynamic threshold, respectively. Equating LTP/LTD with one \(NMDA/\mathrm{Ca}^{2+}\) pathway even though mechanisms vary across synapses and contexts. Using only coincident high activity in basic Hebbian learning and overlooking centered covariance and depression. Treating an eigenvector as a particular neuron. Claiming that covariance “must be positive” without writing a quadratic-form proof of PSD. Confusing directional selection with stabilization of the norm. Equating Hebbian learning with PCA without stating its assumptions. Assuming dopamine is the third factor in every form of reward learning. The Hebbian-learning/PCA relationship holds only under particular linear, statistical, and stabilizing assumptions; “Hebbian = PCA” is not a universal identity. STDP timing rule ∆\(w = f (t_{\mathrm{post}} - t_{\mathrm{pre}} )\) Pair-based approximation Basic rate Hebbian rule \(\tau w\) ẇi = hxi With nonnegative activity, it only potentiates Expected dynamics of centered Hebbian learning \(\tau w\) \(E[\dot{w}] = Cw\) Linear neuron with stationary inputs Positive semidefiniteness of covariance vT Cv ≥ 0 Finite second moments Hebbian eigenmode growth \(\dot{a}k = (\lambda _{k} /\tau w )\)ak Fixed C Oja's rule \(\dot{w}i \propto  hxi - h_{2}\) wi Online approximation to PCA BCM sign switch ẇi ∝ hxi (h − θ) Dynamic threshold long-term potentiation, LTP A lasting increase in synaptic efficacy. long-term depression, LTD A lasting decrease in synaptic efficacy. spike-timing-dependent plasticity, STDP An empirical rule in which weight change depends on relative pre/post spike timing. Hebbian learning A class of rules in which coordinated activity drives changes in connectivity. covariance rule A plasticity rule driven by centered pre- and postsynaptic fluctuations. principal eigenvector The direction associated with the largest covariance eigenvalue. synaptic scaling Global rescaling that maintains an overall activity or weight range. Oja rule A Hebbian PCA rule with a local normalization term. BCM rule A rule that uses a sliding postsynaptic threshold to control LTP and LTD. three-factor rule An update determined jointly by presynaptic activity, postsynaptic activity, and a third modulatory or teaching signal. Why is a classical STDP window not interchangeable with a firing-rate covariance rule? STDP preserves millisecond relative timing between pre- and postsynaptic spikes, whereas a covariance rule averages activity fluctuations over a longer window. They can be related under specific statistical and timescale assumptions, but they use different state variables, experimental protocols, and levels of mechanistic interpretation. Hebb's original proposal links coincident activity to stronger connectivity. Experimentally, high-frequency stimulation of the CA3-to-CA1 pathway can induce long-term potentiation (LTP), whereas a low-frequency protocol can induce long-term depression (LTD). Both describe persistent changes in synaptic efficacy after induction. Neither is the same as transient facilitation, and a single response curve cannot establish one unique molecular mechanism. Why does a negative off-diagonal covariance entry not violate positive semidefiniteness? Positive semidefiniteness constrains the variance \(v^\mathrm{T}Cv\) along every complete direction, not each matrix entry separately. Two variables can be anticorrelated, giving \(C_{ij}<0\), while every linear combination still has a variance equal to an expected square. Covariance is symmetric because \(C_{ij}=E[(x_{i}-\mu _{i})(x_{j}-\mu _{j})]\), and exchanging the two scalar factors leaves their product unchanged. It is also positive semidefinite (PSD): for every v, the quadratic form \(v^\mathrm{T}Cv\) is the expected square of the projection \(v^\mathrm{T}(x-\mu )\). PSD does not require every off-diagonal entry to be positive. Anticorrelated variables may have negative covariance while the full quadratic form remains nonnegative. Why is it inadequate to reduce a reward-based three-factor rule to “Hebbian learning multiplied by dopamine”? The third factor may encode reward, reward-prediction error, an error signal, context, or another neuromodulatory gate. Its timing, receptors, eligibility trace, and specificity for the target weight all affect learning, so dopamine is only one candidate implementation in some systems. The BCM rule changes the sign of plasticity using a postsynaptic sliding threshold, for example \(dw_{i}/dt\propto h x_{i}(h-\theta )\), while \(\theta\) adapts to recent \(h^2\). With \(h<\theta\), the same presynaptic activity tends toward LTD; with \(h>\theta\), it tends toward LTP. Sustained higher activity raises \(\theta\) and makes potentiation harder to trigger. Unlike Oja's explicit weight decay, BCM creates competition and stability through an activity-dependent sign switch. Which interpretation is supported by the schematic “Oja's Rule Selects the Principal Statistical Direction While Bounding Weight Norm”? For centered linear input, the Oja update combines the Hebbian term h x and weight-dependent decay \(-h^{2}w\) in one local rule. The first rotates w toward high-variance directions of the input covariance, while the second strengthens as output grows, allowing the direction to approach the principal eigenvector without unbounded norm growth. This conclusion assumes stationary input, a suitably small learning rate, and a nondegenerate largest eigenvalue.

title: Lecture 11: Machine Learning: Regression, Gradient Descent, and Backpropagation
subtitle: Machine Learning: Regression, Gradient Descent, and Backpropagation
text:
Machine Learning: Regression, Gradient Descent, and Backpropagation Dataset (x,y) → architecture → loss → gradient descent → linear regression → closed form Define a supervised-learning problem in terms of its dataset, architecture, loss, and learning rule, and distinguish the target support of classification from that of regression. Use a first-order Taylor expansion to explain why the gradient is the locally steepest ascent direction and why a step along the negative gradient reduces squared loss. Derive the linear-regression gradient, its Hebbian-like and stabilizing components, and the normal equation step by step, including how to handle a singular design matrix. Explain why a deep linear network has a linear input-output map even though its multilayer factorization produces nonlinear and generally nonconvex optimization dynamics. Derive the backpropagated error recurrence and each layer's weight gradient by tracking shapes, while treating backpropagation as a training algorithm rather than an established neurobiological mechanism. A machine-learning problem must specify its representation or architecture, objective or loss, and optimization or learning rule. Linear regression is the transparent example: the squared-error gradient decomposes into a data-dependent Hebbian-like term and a weight-dependent stabilizing term and admits a normal-equation closed form. In a deep network, backpropagation repeatedly applies the chain rule, carrying output error through transposed weights and local activation derivatives to each layer. Conflating architecture, loss, and optimizer. Forgetting that the gradient points uphill and the update needs a negative sign. Omitting matrix shapes and therefore misplacing transposes in matrix calculus. Attempting a direct inverse for a singular design matrix. Assuming optimization of a deep linear network is itself linear or convex. Treating backpropagation as an established biological synaptic mechanism. Reading an informal historical aside as a rigorous technical conclusion. Do not describe backpropagation as a biological mechanism in which error is directly sent back to neurons. Label it as a training algorithm and distinguish its formal resemblance to three-factor plasticity from its mechanistic differences. Gradient descent ∆\(w = -\eta 
abla w L\) \(\eta >0\) and a local step Linear-regression loss 1 \(L= \Vert y - X T w\Vert 2 2P\) Source orientation X:N×P Least-squares gradient \(
abla w\) \(L = -X(y - X T w)/P\) Differentiable squared loss Closed-form solution ŵ = (XX T )−1 Xy Invertible \(XX^\mathrm{T}\) Backpropagated-error recurrence \(\delta  (\ell ) = (W (\ell +1)T \delta  (\ell +1) ) \odot  \varphi '\) Compatible shapes Layer weight gradient \(\partial L/\partial W (\ell ) = \delta  (\ell )\) \(z (\ell -1)T\) One example; average over the batch afterward supervised learning Learning a predictor from input-target pairs. classification Prediction of a discrete label. regression Prediction of a continuous target. architecture The connectivity and computations defining a model. loss function An objective quantifying disagreement between prediction and target. gradient The vector of parameter derivatives pointing in the direction of fastest local increase. learning rate The scale of each gradient step. normal equation The linear equation satisfied by a least-squares optimum. backpropagation An algorithm for efficiently computing multilayer chain-rule gradients. local derivative The derivative of one computational node's output with respect to its input. Why is the statement “the gradient points toward the minimum” inaccurate? The gradient points in the locally steepest ascent direction at the current point; its negative is the local descent direction. It uses only first-order information at that location and does not directly identify a distant global minimum. Supervised learning supplies input-target pairs. In handwritten-digit recognition, x is an image and y is a discrete digit label, making the task classification. In optic-flow estimation, x may be two adjacent frames and y a continuous motion vector at each location, making it regression. Both require a clear account of how training examples are sampled and whether test examples follow the same distribution. Why can training every layer of a deep linear network not be treated as ordinary convex linear regression, even though the overall mapping is linear? The product \(W^L\cdots W^0\) defines a linear mapping, but it is a multilinear product of the component layer parameters. Scale and factorization are nonunique, and updates to different layers depend on one another, so optimization in parameter space is generally nonconvex. Expanding the gradient gives \(

The first term writes input-target coactivity into the weights; the second grows with the current weights and input covariance, providing stabilization. Its form resembles biological Hebbian learning, but a target y, batch access, and signed error are not ordinary local coactivity. Why does the backpropagated error recurrence use the transpose of the downstream weight matrix? The forward map W carries hidden coordinates into downstream coordinates. The chain rule must aggregate downstream scalar sensitivities back into each hidden coordinate, which is exactly the reverse Jacobian product \(W^\mathrm{T}\delta\); its shape also returns from the downstream dimension to the hidden dimension. Each weight \(W^{(\ell -1)}_{ij}\) contributes presynaptic activation \(z^{(\ell -1)}_j\) to postsynaptic preactivation \(h^{(\ell )}_i\). title: Lecture 12: Introduction to Vision: Hierarchy, Receptive Fields, and LNP Models
subtitle: Introduction to Vision: Hierarchy, Receptive Fields, and LNP Models
text: Introduction to Vision: Hierarchy, Receptive Fields, and LNP Models Retina→V1→streams → contrast → LNP → DoG center-surround → rectified feature maps → Gabor orientation Use the course-level photoreceptor–RGC–V1–MT/IT/LIP diagram to explain the visual hierarchy while separating anatomical pathways, receptive-field computations, and functional labels. Explain every stage of the LNP model—linear filter, static nonlinearity, and conditional Poisson output—and why early vision is commonly modeled in terms of contrast rather than raw luminance. Construct ON and OFF Difference-of-Gaussians receptive fields through spatial convolution and predict the response signs for a uniform field, a center spot, and surround illumination. Decompose a Gabor kernel into its Gaussian envelope, carrier frequency, orientation, and phase; then explain how the subsequent static nonlinearity introduces thresholding and saturation in V1 simple-cell orientation tuning. Extend receptive fields into space-time, distinguish separable from nonseparable kernels, and infer direction selectivity from slope in an x-t diagram. The visual hierarchy is not merely an anatomical list but a computational organization in which receptive-field size, feature complexity, history dependence, and invariance change by stage. LNP first projects a stimulus onto a linear receptive field, maps the drive through a nonlinearity to a rate, and uses a Poisson process to describe spikes. DoG, Gabor, and nonseparable spatiotemporal kernels summarize center-surround, orientation, and motion selectivity. Treating a receptive field only as a geometric region in visual space. Using raw luminance and contrast interchangeably. Leaving the sign or flip convention of a convolution kernel unstated. Assuming a feature map is a copy of the original image rather than a map of filter responses. Confusing Gabor orientation, phase, and spatial frequency. Assuming a separable spatiotemporal receptive field is automatically direction-selective. Equating an anatomical hierarchy with one purely feedforward computation. Do not describe a receptive field only as a screen “location”; it is a stimulus-response relationship. Distinguish a linear receptive field, classical receptive field, and experimental definition. Sparse-noise receptive-field mapping provides a useful transfer example. Visual contrast \(s = (I - I_{0} )/I_{0}\) \(I_{0}>0\) Linear receptive-field drive \(L=K \ast s\) Linear shift-invariant approximation Static nonlinearity \(r = F(L)\) A nonnegative or saturating rate, as specified LNP spike generation \(n \sim  \operatorname{Poisson}(rT )\) Conditional Poisson process Center-surround receptive field KDoG = Gcenter − Gsurround A wider surround Simple-cell orientation filter KGabor = G(x′, y ′ ) cos(kx′ + ϕ) Localized sinusoid Separable receptive field \(K(x, y, t) = Ks\) Kt Rank-1 space-time structure receptive field A local or functional relation between a stimulus pattern and a response, not merely a screen location. feature selectivity A preferential response to a class of stimulus structures. dorsal stream A broad visual pathway associated with motion- and action-related processing. ventral stream A broad visual pathway associated with processing related to object identity. linear-nonlinear-Poisson model, \(\ln P A\) cascade of a linear filter, nonlinearity, and Poisson spike-count variability. center-surround A receptive-field organization with opposite signs in the center and periphery. feature map The rectified response of one filter at every location. Gabor kernel A Gaussian-windowed sinusoid. separable Having space and time components that can be written as a product. direction selectivity A preferential response to one direction of motion. Why is “ON cells prefer light and OFF cells prefer dark” an incomplete account of a center-surround receptive field? The response depends on contrast location and surround context. A bright spot in an ON center can excite, whereas a bright surround can cancel it. A balanced kernel may not respond to the same global luminance, so both polarity and spatial pattern must be specified. Place photoreceptors, retinal ganglion cells (RGCs), V1, MT, IT, and LIP on a hierarchy diagram. The retina first encodes local contrast; V1 emphasizes local structure such as orientation; MT and the dorsal stream are associated with motion and action-relevant variables; IT and the ventral stream with object features; and LIP often with decision-related representations. This computational map does not imply exclusively one-way feedforward information flow. Why does changing Gabor phase \(\phi\) not change preferred orientation \(\theta\)? \(\phi\) translates positive and negative lobes along a fixed carrier axis and determines whether a bright or dark edge aligns with the filter. \(\theta\) rotates the coordinate system and determines which edge or grating direction aligns with the elongated lobes. V1 simple-cell receptive fields often contain alternating elongated ON and OFF lobes. A Gabor kernel uses a Gaussian envelope to localize position and size and a cosine carrier to create the alternating lobes. \(\theta\) rotates the coordinates, k controls spatial frequency, and \(\phi\) controls phase. Orientation tuning arises because positive contributions add when an edge aligns with the lobes, whereas an orthogonal edge straddles positive and negative regions and cancels. Why does a biphasic temporal kernel not automatically guarantee direction selectivity? If the kernel still factors into a fixed spatial profile and a temporal waveform, it only reweights one spatial feature over time and never pairs distinct locations with particular lags. Direction selectivity requires space-time nonseparability or an equivalent multichannel nonlinear computation. A vertical edge moving rightward at velocity v satisfies \(x(t)=x_{0}+vt\). In an x-t diagram it is an oblique line of slope \(dx/dt=v\).
