If the positive lobes of a receptive field lie along the same line, the edge traverses every positive zone in sequence and produces a large inner product. An edge moving the other way follows the opposite slope and encounters mismatched positive and negative zones. Which interpretation is supported by the schematic “From ON/OFF Local-Contrast Channels to an Oriented Gabor-Like Receptive Field”? ON/OFF center-surround filters first recode absolute luminance as local contrast. Arranging several polarity-specific subfields along one axis makes signed contributions add for the matching direction and cancel for an orthogonal direction, creating an elongated, orientation-selective Gabor-like linear receptive field. The diagram distinguishes local DoG contrast computation from the later subfield arrangement that creates orientation tuning.

title: Lecture 13: Spike-Triggered Average and White-Noise System Identification
subtitle: Spike-Triggered Average and White-Noise System Identification
text: Spike-Triggered Average and White-Noise System Identification White-noise stimulus → spike-triggered ensemble → matrix notation → least squares/Hessian → white covariance → STA proportionality Organize white-noise stimuli, spike trains, and the spike-triggered ensemble into a system-identification workflow, distinguishing a descriptive STA, a filter estimator, and a complete LNP component. Move among continuous convolution, pixel-index summation, and matrix notation while tracking the shapes of S, K, L, and the count vector and the orientation of the time-lag axis. Derive the normal equation and Hessian from mean-squared loss for a linear neuron, and explain circular versus elongated loss contours through stimulus covariance. Starting from \(SS^\mathrm{T}\approx T\sigma _{s}^2I\), derive the proportionality between \(\hat{K}\) and the STA while retaining the scaling by spike count, bin width, and stimulus variance. Recover a static nonlinearity with the small-bin Poisson approximation and diagnose STA failure caused by multiple features, an even nonlinearity, colored stimuli, or insufficient data. STA is both a descriptive average and, under a linear model, Gaussian white stimulation, and a suitable nonlinearity, a filter estimator. Matrix least squares reveals why: white stimulation makes the design covariance approximately a scalar identity, reducing the normal equation to a stimulus-response correlation. Recovering the nonlinearity yields an LNP model that can predict new stimuli, but multiple relevant dimensions, even-symmetric nonlinearities, or correlated stimulation can make the STA zero or biased. Treating the STA only as an image average without specifying time-lag alignment. Leaving matrix orientation unstated and confusing \(S^\mathrm{T}K\) with KS. Omitting the large-sample and equal-variance assumptions behind white covariance. Equating STA amplitude unconditionally with physical filter gain. Concluding from \(STA=0\) that a neuron has no receptive field. Forgetting to divide by bin width when recovering F. Evaluating a model on its training fit instead of held-out prediction. Distinguish the STA as a descriptive average, linear-filter estimator, and LNP-model component. They are related under particular assumptions, not unconditionally equivalent. Pixelized linear drive \(L = ST K S\):P×T Least-squares filter K̂ = (SS T )−1 Sh Invertible \(SS^\mathrm{T}\) Loss Hessian \(H = SS T /T\) Linear squared loss White-noise covariance SS \(T \approx  T \sigma s_{2} I\) Large T with independent equal-variance pixels Spike-triggered average 1 X \(ST A = st\) nsp t∈spikes Aligned stimulus histories STA/filter relation \(\hat{K} \propto  ST A\) White Gaussian single-filter assumptions Small-bin nonlinearity estimate P (spike|L) ≈ ∆\(tF (L)\) \(\Delta t\) rate≪1 system identification Inferring a system model from input-output data. white noise An ideal random stimulus with uncorrelated dimensions or time bins and uniform power. spike-triggered ensemble The collection of stimulus histories preceding all spikes. spike-triggered average, STA The mean of the spike-triggered ensemble. design matrix A matrix organizing stimulus vectors by examples or time bins. Hessian The matrix of second derivatives of loss with respect to parameters. isotropic Having equal curvature or variance in every direction. whitening Removing covariance correlations to obtain variables near unit covariance. correlated stimulus A stimulus whose dimensions have nonzero covariance. relevant dimension A stimulus-projection direction on which the response depends. Why must each member of the spike-triggered ensemble contain a stimulus history rather than only the frame in which the spike occurs? Neural responses have latency and may depend on multiple past lags. Using only the current frame discards temporal filtering and attaches the causal feature to the wrong spike time. A history vector permits simultaneous estimation of spatial and temporal receptive-field structure. System identification reverses forward prediction. A forward LNP model predicts spikes from known K and F; the experiment supplies stimulus s and spikes k and seeks K and F. A standard protocol presents random checkerboard white noise, records neural spikes, looks backward from every spike over the same time lags, and averages those stimulus histories. Stimulus coordinates, frame duration, and neural latency must be defined first. Why does an elongated loss contour indicate that some filter combinations are estimated unreliably? Moving along the ellipse's long axis raises loss only slightly. This is a small-eigenvalue direction of the Hessian, where many different K values make similar predictions on the sampled stimuli, allowing finite noise to shift the minimum substantially. For a linear model with quadratic loss, the Hessian \(H=SS^\mathrm{T}/T\) is independent of K. Its eigenvectors are the principal axes of the loss ellipse and its eigenvalues are curvatures. Along a large-eigenvalue direction, a small change in K noticeably changes predictions and the data tightly constrain the minimum. Along a small-eigenvalue direction, the loss is flat and recording noise, finite samples, or regularization can move the estimate substantially. Why is a smooth increasing \(\hat{F}(L)\) curve on the training data insufficient evidence that an LNP model predicts? Both K and F were estimated from the same data, and binning plus a flexible curve can absorb noise. Generalization must be tested by computing projections on held-out stimuli and predicting conditional rates or spikes there. After estimating \(\hat{K}\), compute \(L_{t}=\hat{K}^\mathrm{T}s_{t}\) in every time bin, group values into bins of L, and estimate empirical \(P(\mathrm{spike}|L)\). The small-bin Poisson approximation gives \(P(k=1|L)\approx \Delta tF(L)\), hence \(\hat{F}(L)=P(\mathrm{spike}|L)/\Delta t\). Finally combine \(\hat{K}\), \(\hat{F}\), and the Poisson stage on held-out stimuli and compare predicted with observed spikes; a training STA alone is not a model test. Which interpretation is supported by the schematic “Forward LNP Prediction and Reverse STA Estimation Form One Validation Workflow”? A forward LNP model projects stimulus history onto \(L=k^{\mathrm{T}}s\), transforms it through \(F(L)\) into a conditional firing rate, and generates spikes. Reverse analysis aligns and averages the stimulus history before each spike. For zero-mean white Gaussian input, one relevant dimension, and sufficient data, STA points along k. Colored input, an even nonlinearity, or multiple relevant dimensions breaks this simple relation.

title: Lecture 14: Spike-Triggered Covariance and Generalized Linear Models
subtitle: Spike-Triggered Covariance and Generalized Linear Models
text: Spike-Triggered Covariance and Generalized Linear Models Multiple features → STC eigenspace → stimulus correction → GLM distribution → linear predictor → link Explain why one STA cannot describe an H1-like or complex-cell-like response driven by multiple features, and use spike-triggered covariance eigenvectors to find stimulus directions whose variance changes. Define the response distribution, linear predictor, and link function of a GLM, including the relation between the canonical parameter and the mean. Write the log likelihoods for Gaussian, Poisson, and Bernoulli probability models and explain the supports enforced by identity, log, and logit links. Strictly separate Poisson counts, small-bin Bernoulli spike/no-spike observations, and logistic classification so their likelihoods and interpretations are not conflated. Reconstruct the stimulus, self-history, and coupling filters of a retinal population GLM, and explain why fitted coupling provides conditional prediction rather than proof of a direct synapse. STC compares spike-triggered covariance with raw stimulus covariance to find directions in which pre-spike variance expands or contracts; colored stimulation requires whitening or correction. A GLM unifies several regressions through a response distribution, linear predictor, and link. A retinal population GLM can fit stimulus filters, self-history, and cross-neuron coupling together, but remains a statistical model: a coupling filter is not automatically a direct synapse. Concluding from \(STA=0\) that there is no relevant feature. Applying ordinary eigendecomposition directly to \(\Delta C\) under colored stimulation. Interpreting “linear” in GLM as requiring a linear response mean. Using an identity link for Poisson data and thereby allowing a negative rate. Conflating Bernoulli logistic classification with a Poisson small-count model. Treating fitted coupling filters as direct anatomical synapses. Ignoring history dependence and thereby biasing the apparent stimulus filter. Do not read “linear” in GLM as a requirement that the response mean be linear. The predictor is linear; the link determines its relation to the mean. STC covariance change ∆C = Cspike − Cstim Centered ensembles GLM linear predictor \(\eta  = X\beta \) Shape-compatible design Link function \(g(E[y|x]) = \eta \) Chosen response family Inverse Poisson log link \(\lambda  = e\eta \) Positive mean Inverse logistic link \(q = (1 + e^{-\eta } )-1\) \(0<q<1\) Poisson log likelihood ℓP ois = (yη − eη − log y!) Conditionally independent bins or counts Logistic loss −ℓBern = cross-entropy Bernoulli outcomes spike-triggered covariance, STC Analysis of covariance in the spike-triggered ensemble. relevant subspace The response-sensitive subspace spanned by several stimulus filters. exponential family A family of distributions expressible in a specified canonical statistic-parameter form. linear predictor \(\eta =X\beta\). link function The mapping between a conditional mean and \(\eta\). Poisson regression A log-link GLM for a count or rate. logistic regression A logit-link GLM for a Bernoulli outcome. log odds \(\log[q/(1-q)]\). history filter The linear effect of past spikes on the current conditional response. coupling filter A predictive filter applied to the histories of other units. Why cannot the sign of an STC eigenvector say whether a stimulus is excitatory or inhibitory? Covariance describes an unoriented axis. v and -v have identical squared projections and covariance. To learn how projection sign affects rate, fit or inspect the nonlinearity along that axis. Use the blowfly H1 neuron as an example: its stimulus \(s(t)=v(t)\) is image velocity rather than a two-dimensional light pattern. The response may depend on projections through several temporal filters \(K_{1}\cdots K_{n}\) followed by a multidimensional nonlinearity F. Thus stimulus-vector coordinates are defined by the question: they may be pixels, velocity history, past spikes, or other measured covariates. Why is the identity link \(\lambda =\eta\) structurally unsuitable for \(a \operatorname{Poisson} GLM\)? The linear predictor \(\eta\) may be any real number, so an identity link permits negative expected counts. The log link \(\lambda =e^\eta\) maps the whole real line to positive means and yields the convenient residual gradient of the canonical Poisson likelihood. For a unit-variance Gaussian model with identity link, \(m=\eta =x^\mathrm{T}\beta\). The β-dependent part of the log likelihood is \(-1/2\Sigma (y-m)^2\), so likelihood maximization equals mean-squared-error minimization. Unknown or heteroscedastic variance requires an extension; squared loss is not the only model for continuous responses. Why does fitting stimulus and coupling filters jointly still not justify interpreting a coupling coefficient as a causal synapse? The model controls only measured covariates. Unobserved common input, global state, model mismatch, and indirect network paths can still create conditional dependence. Establishing a causal synapse additionally requires intervention, anatomy, or stronger identifiability assumptions. In a very small bin, \(y_{t}\in {0,1}\) and a Bernoulli likelihood is suitable. Use log odds \(\theta =\log[q/(1-q)]\) as predictor \(\eta\), with inverse link \(q=e^\eta /(1+e^\eta )\). At \(\eta =0\), \(q=0.5\); increasing \(\eta\) by one multiplies the odds by e. That statement is more accurate than a fixed probability increment because sigmoid slope differs near 0 and near 1. Which interpretation is supported by the schematic “A Population GLM Places Stimulus, Self-History, and Coupling in One Conditional Predictor”? A population GLM adds a stimulus filter, self-history filter, and cross-neuron coupling filters in predictor \(\eta _{i}(t)\), then uses a log or logit inverse link to produce a nonnegative rate or binary spike probability. Simultaneous fitting reduces omitted-covariate confounding, but a coupling coefficient still denotes predictive dependence conditional on the included variables, not an anatomical synapse.

title: Lecture 15: Efficient Coding and Information Theory
subtitle: Efficient Coding and Information Theory
text: Efficient Coding and Information Theory Barlow hypotheses → surprise \(-\log p\)→ entropy → mutual information → Gaussian channel → redundancy/capacity Distinguish Barlow's three hypotheses accurately and present efficient coding as a normative proposal constrained by noise and resources. Explain surprise=\(-\log p\) from the additivity of information for independent events, and compute entropy, conditional entropy, and mutual information. Derive the joint-distribution form of mutual information, show that \(I=0\) under independence, and explain why differential entropy can be negative and depends on coordinate units. Starting from \(x=s+\eta _{x}\) and \(y=Ax+\eta _{y}\), derive input and output covariance while distinguishing signal, input noise, and output noise by their locations in the encoder. Explain the Gaussian-MI determinant formula, fixed-information constraints, channel capacity, decorrelation, and orthogonal nonuniqueness, and show how added symmetries can select center-surround filters. Barlow's efficient coding is a normative hypothesis: under resource and noise constraints, a sensory system should reduce predictable redundancy while retaining useful information. Information theory quantifies predictability and transmission through surprise, entropy, and mutual information. Atick and Redlich model the retina as a noisy linear encoder and decoder that lowers redundancy under fixed-information and output-capacity constraints. Decorrelation is nonunique; rotational symmetry together with locality and related constraints can select a center-surround form. Treating efficient coding as a uniquely established mechanism rather than a normative hypothesis. Equating entropy unconditionally with useful information. Calling a negative differential entropy an error. Assuming \(MI=0\) means only zero linear correlation; when well-defined, it means independence. Optimizing only decorrelation while ignoring noise and output capacity. Assuming that the whitening solution is unique. Presenting the normative center-surround prediction as singular causal evidence. Distinguish entropy, differential entropy, mutual information, redundancy, and channel capacity. Avoid unconditional claims such as “more entropy is better.” Surprise \(S(x) = - \log p(x)\) Chosen logarithm base Entropy \(H(X) = E[- \log p(X)]\) Discrete distribution Mutual information \(I(X; Y ) = H(X) - H(X|Y )\) Known joint distribution Dependence form of MI \(\sum  p(x, y)\) \(I= p(x, y)\) \(\log p(x)p(y)\) Support handled correctly Linear Gaussian covariance propagation Cy = ACx \(AT + \sigma y_{2}\) I Independent additive output noise Gaussian-MI determinant form 1 det Cy \(I(X; Y ) = \log 2 \det Cy|x\) Jointly Gaussian variables Decorrelation objective Cout ≈ diagonal Second-order redundancy efficient coding A normative principle for optimizing an information representation under resource and noise constraints. redundancy Structure that is predictable from other components and transmitted repeatedly. surprise The −log probability of an event. entropy Average surprise or uncertainty. conditional entropy Residual uncertainty after another variable is given. mutual information The reduction in uncertainty about one variable supplied by another. differential entropy An entropy-like quantity for a continuous density that can be negative and depends on units. channel capacity The maximum mutual information attainable under input constraints. decorrelation Making off-diagonal covariance entries approach zero. normative model A model of what a system should optimize rather than a direct specification of mechanism. Why does negative differential entropy not mean probability theory has failed? A continuous density is not the probability of one outcome; it may exceed 1, and its entropy contains the coordinate bin size or units. Rescaling a variable adds a log-scale term. Shared scale contributions cancel in MI, which remains nonnegative and retains its dependence interpretation. Barlow's framework contributes three ideas: detect “passwords” of critical significance, filter signals for other nervous-system regions, and recode sensory messages to reduce redundancy. Focus on the third. Efficient coding explains why a code is advantageous under specified input statistics, noise, and cost. It is a normative hypothesis; the same receptive field may also have developmental, biophysical, or task-specific explanations. Why does moving input and output noise into one term before A change the optimization? A reshapes input noise, so increasing gain at one frequency also amplifies its input noise. Output noise does not pass through A, and increasing gain can improve signal relative to output noise. Their effects on the gain tradeoff differ and cannot be merged. Assuming signal and noises are zero-mean and mutually independent, \(C_{x}=C_{s}+C_{\eta _{x}}\). A linear transformation yields \(AC_{x}A^\mathrm{T}\), after which output noise adds: \(C_{y}=A(C_{s}+C_{\eta _{x}})A^\mathrm{T}+C_{\eta _{y}}\). Input noise is amplified or attenuated together with the signal, while output noise never passes through A; optimal gain therefore cannot be based on signal covariance alone. What crucial conditions are missing from the statement “decorrelation produces center-surround filters”? Decorrelation requires only a diagonal or whitened output covariance, and any subsequent orthogonal rotation satisfies it equally well. Translation and rotation symmetry, locality, wiring, noise, or cost constraints are needed to select center-surround filters from the equivalent solutions. A whitening transform V satisfies \(VC_{x}V^\mathrm{T}=I\). For any orthogonal U, \((UV)C_{x}(UV)^\mathrm{T}=UIU^\mathrm{T}=I\), so the pre-output-noise whitened code may be rotated without changing covariance. Full Gaussian MI is also unchanged only if output noise is isotropic, \(C_{\eta _{y}}=\sigma _{y}^{2}I\), or absent; then total and conditional-noise covariances undergo the same orthogonal similarity transformation. With anisotropic output noise, rotating the encoder changes signal alignment with the noise axes and generally changes MI. Decorrelation alone therefore identifies a family of solutions, not a unique localized center-surround shape for each neuron. Which interpretation is supported by the schematic “Redundancy Reduction in a Noisy Sensory Channel Must Respect Fidelity and Output-Cost Constraints”? Encoder A transforms signal and input noise together, whereas output noise enters after A. A diagonal output covariance alone therefore does not guarantee useful coding. In the Atick–Redlich framework, redundancy is reduced subject to retained-information and output-power or dynamic-range constraints. Whitening removes second-order correlations, but any orthogonal rotation preserves whitened covariance; localized center-surround filters require additional assumptions such as symmetry and locality.

title: Lecture 16: Adaptation, Natural Scene Statistics, and Fourier Analysis
subtitle: Adaptation, Natural Scene Statistics, and Fourier Analysis
text: Adaptation, Natural Scene Statistics, and Fourier Analysis SNR → center-surround adaptation → translation invariance → Fourier basis → convolution theorem → power spectrum Explain from the relative strengths of input signal and noise why decorrelating filters are appropriate at high SNR while spatial averaging serves a different objective at low SNR. Express translation-invariant image statistics as a correlation function of displacement alone and explain why complex exponentials are the natural basis of convolution operators. Derive the convolution theorem and output power-spectrum equation step by step, then infer the frequency trend of a whitening filter from the approximate natural-image spectrum \(1/|\xi |^{2}\). Design an LNP comparison across illumination levels or stimulus statistics that separates a change in the linear filter, a change in the static nonlinearity, and a mere response-scale change. The central prediction of Atick–Redlich theory is not one fixed filter but a filter that changes with SNR: high SNR permits strong decorrelation, while low SNR favors spatial averaging and denoising. Approximate translation invariance of natural scenes makes covariance depend only on displacement, allowing Fourier modes to diagonalize convolution and covariance. Natural-image power falls approximately with inverse squared spatial frequency. Perfect whitening would boost high frequencies, but optics, photoreceptors, and noise suppress excessive high-frequency gain. Treating the Fourier transform as a table of physically meaningless formulas. Confusing spatial-frequency magnitude, orientation, and phase. Assuming complex numbers introduce an additional biological variable; they are a representational tool. Using the convolution theorem without a normalization or sign convention. Treating \(1/|\xi |^{2}\) as an exact law for every image. Letting perfect whitening amplify high frequencies without bound while ignoring optics and noise. Comparing only firing rates in an adaptation experiment and not the filter or nonlinearity. Do not teach the Fourier transform as a formula table. Always explain the physical meaning of spatial frequency for an image and receptive field, and state what amplitude and phase each represent. Signal-to-noise ratio SN \(R = S/N\) One frequency and measurement convention Translation-invariant covariance \(C(\rho _{1}, \rho _{2} ) = C(\rho _{1} - \rho _{2} )\) Stationary field Fourier transform \(\hat{s}(\xi ) = e^{-i2\pi \xi }\cdot x s(x)dx\) Chosen normalization Euler's identity ei\(\theta  = \cos \theta  + i \sin \theta \) Complex representation Convolution theorem \ \(K \ast  s = \hat{K}\) \(\hat{s}\) Linear shift-invariant filtering Power spectrum \(P (\xi ) = E[|\hat{s}(\xi )|2 ]\) Ensemble or time average Perfect-whitening magnitude −1/2 |K̂| ∝ Pin No additional noise or cost adaptation A change in response or model parameters with stimulus statistics or state. signal-to-noise ratio, SNR Signal magnitude or power relative to noise. translation invariance Statistics or an operator that do not depend on absolute position. spatial frequency Sinusoidal cycles per unit distance; the vector also encodes direction. Fourier transform A conversion between position and frequency representations. complex \(\operatorname{exponential} A\) unified representation of sine/cosine amplitude and phase. power spectrum Mean squared amplitude of each frequency component. whitening Making an output spectrum or covariance approximately flat or identity. low-pass Preserving low frequencies while suppressing high frequencies. aliasing Undersampling that makes a high frequency appear as a lower one. Why should a weaker surround in low light not be summarized as the visual system “no longer caring about edges”? Edges can remain behaviorally important. The change means that current high-frequency evidence is unreliable relative to noise and strong differencing would amplify noise. The system temporarily sacrifices resolution for a more stable estimate; the behavioral target need not have changed. Interpret filter shape along an SNR axis. At high SNR, input detail is reliable relative to internal and photon noise. Neighboring pixels are then strongly correlated, and transmitting them unchanged wastes limited output dynamic range on repeated information. An excitatory-center, inhibitory-surround difference kernel suppresses common slow components while retaining edges, reducing output correlations. A strong surround is a normative prediction under specified statistics and costs; it does not alone establish its synaptic implementation. Why do Fourier modes “diagonalize” a translation-invariant linear filter? After convolution, each input mode \(e^{i\xi \cdot x}\) remains the same \(\xi\) and is multiplied only by complex number \(\hat{K}(\xi )\); distinct \(\xi\) never mix. In this basis, the operator is represented by diagonal gains, one per mode. A two-dimensional component \(e^{i\xi \cdot x}\) carries frequency direction and phase. The dot product \(\xi \cdot x\) projects position onto the frequency vector. Phase changes fastest along \(\xi\) and remains constant in the perpendicular direction, so visible stripes are perpendicular to \(\xi\). A real image uses paired \(+\xi\) and \(-\xi\) components whose imaginary parts cancel. Near the spectrum center are slow variations; farther away are finer spatial structures. Why must an LNP filter's scale convention be fixed before comparing two adaptation conditions? Multiplying k by constant a while dividing the nonlinearity's horizontal axis by a gives identical firing predictions. Without fixing ||k|| or another convention, an apparent gain change can be only parameterization nonuniqueness. This turns this prediction into an LNP measurement. Present sufficiently rich stimuli under high and low light or different spatial correlations, estimate filter \(k_{c}\) separately, and then estimate each condition's nonlinearity \(f_{c}\). Fix a normalization before comparing filters—for example \(||k_{c}||=1\) with signs aligned by the dominant lobe—because multiplying k by a constant and inversely scaling the input axis of f gives identical predictions. Then compare spatial profile, Fourier gain, integrated center-surround ratio, and cross-condition prediction. Which interpretation is supported by the schematic “Noise Truncates the Ideal High-Frequency Gain of Natural-Image Whitening”? If natural-image power is approximated by \(P_{\mathrm{in}}(\xi )\propto 1/|\xi |^{2}\) and noise and gain limits are temporarily ignored, flattening \(P_{\mathrm{out}}=|\hat{K}|^{2}P_{\mathrm{in}}\) requires \(|\hat{K}|\propto |\xi |\). Real optics attenuate extreme high-frequency signal without eliminating approximately flat output noise, so a noise-aware filter rolls off at high frequencies. When SNR falls further, the reliable band narrows and favors pooling. All three curves are normalized theoretical sketches, not empirical measurements.

title: Lecture 17: Visual Networks: Cascades, Complex Cells, and Recurrence
subtitle: Visual Networks: Cascades, Complex Cells, and Recurrence
text: Visual Networks: Cascades, Complex Cells, and Recurrence LNP cascade → simple-cell pooling → complex-cell \(STA=0\)→ quadrature energy → task-optimized models → E/I recurrence Distinguish linear selectivity in simple cells from phase invariance in complex cells, and explain why an even-symmetric response can drive the first-order STA toward zero. Derive phase invariance step by step from the two linear outputs of a quadrature pair while stating the amplitude and orientation dependence that remains. Separate task training of an optimized model from evaluation of neural predictivity, and design a comparison that never leaks test neural data. Write the fixed-point equations and nullclines of an E/I rate network and analyze how surround input can produce suppression without raising inhibitory rate. Use local stability to define an inhibition-stabilized network and avoid reducing ISN to “strong inhibition.” Feedforward cascades can construct selectivity and invariance stage by stage, but descriptive blocks do not automatically identify biological mechanisms. Complex cells are approximately invariant to grating phase, so a single linear STA can be zero; a quadrature-pair square-and-sum energy model is a minimal explanation. Surround suppression likewise is not simply “more inhibition”: recurrent E/I dynamics can make excitation and inhibition fall together, with excitation falling more. Nullclines show the fixed-point shift, while Jacobian stability and an unstable E-only subsystem establish an inhibition-stabilized regime. Treating a descriptive LNP cascade automatically as anatomy or mechanism. Concluding from complex-cell \(STA=0\) that there is no stimulus selectivity. Forgetting that squaring changes sign and phase information. Treating task accuracy and neural predictivity as the same metric. Equating surround suppression with a necessary increase in inhibitory firing or conductance. Reading ISN as meaning that inhibitory rate is always higher. Locating a fixed point without checking its stability. State explicitly that “complex-cell \(STA=0\)” does not mean “no stimulus selectivity”; it is a central counterexample in nonlinear system identification. Motion or orientation energy model \(E = (K_{1} \ast  s)2 + (K_{2} \ast  s)2\) Quadrature filters Phase-invariance identity \(\cos 2 \varphi  + \sin 2 \varphi  = 1\) Ideal pair Linear model-to-neuron mapping \(\hat{r} = Bz\) Fixed features z E/I nullclines \(\dot{r}E = 0\), \(\dot{r}I = 0\) Steady state Rate-network fixed point \(r = F (W r + I)\) Chosen nonlinearities Intuitive ISN criterion E-only unstable + feedback I stable Local effective gain matters cascade Several processing stages composed in sequence. simple cell A classical V1 cell type selective for orientation and sensitive to spatial phase. complex cell A classical V1 cell type selective for orientation but more invariant to phase. quadrature pair Matched filters separated by 90° of phase. energy model A nonlinear model that squares and sums quadrature-filter outputs. neural predictivity How well model features predict neural responses. surround suppression A reduction in center response when the receptive-field surround is stimulated. nullcline A phase-plane curve on which one state derivative equals zero. inhibition-stabilized network, ISN A network whose E subnetwork is unstable alone but stabilized by feedback inhibition. Why does the energy model retain orientation tuning after gaining phase invariance? Phase rotates the matched quadrature outputs in their two-dimensional plane. Changing orientation reduces both filter projections' common amplitude A, so \(A^{2}\) still falls with orientation mismatch. This links cascade models to the Hubel–Wiesel construction. If multiple LGN-like center-surround units are arranged along an oblique axis and pooled with same-sign weights, only a light-dark edge matching that arrangement drives many inputs together, producing an elongated simple-cell receptive field. This construction explains the spatial geometry of orientation selectivity but remains sensitive to light-dark position: translating the same grating by half a period reverses the linear projection. Why is it invalid to repeatedly select the most brain-like network layer on test neural stimuli and report its highest correlation on the same data? Repeated layer selection already uses the test responses. The maximum contains positive selection noise and is biased upward. Choose layers and regularization on validation neural data and perform the final evaluation once on an independent test set. High task accuracy does not define neural similarity. Many internal coordinate systems can implement the same classification boundary; networks that rely on texture or shape may score similarly on labels. Predictivity also depends on mapping flexibility. A nonlinear mapper with far more parameters than observations can fit almost any representation to training responses. Use simple mappings of equal complexity and identical cross-validation for every candidate layer. Why does lower inhibitory-neuron firing after surround not imply that inhibition did not cause surround suppression? A firing rate is the network fixed-point outcome, while inhibitory current also depends on connectivity and presynaptic rate. Surround can first lower E drive and thereby lower I, even though I feedback still determines the fixed point at which E amplification is contained. The ISN has an excitatory subnetwork that would be unstable in isolation—effective recurrent E gain exceeds leak—but fast inhibitory feedback stabilizes the complete E/I network. The name does not mean that inhibitory firing always rises or that every suppression comes from added I input. Under some perturbations, stronger external drive to I lowers its steady-state rate. This paradoxical response arises from network rebalancing and tests ISN structure more directly than simply measuring whether I is large. Which interpretation is supported by the schematic “After Surround Input Shifts the I-Nullcline, Both E and I Can Fall at the Stable Intersection”? In a locally linear E/I rate model, a nullcline intersection is a steady state. Increasing surround drive to the I population shifts the I-nullcline upward. Its new intersection with the fixed E-nullcline can have both lower \(r_{E}\) and lower \(r_{I}\), so surround suppression does not require inhibitory firing to rise. The curves are normalized geometric sketches of the course equations. Full stability still requires Jacobian eigenvalues and cannot be inferred from line intersection alone.

title: Lecture 18: Motor Systems and Linear Neural Dynamics
subtitle: Motor Systems and Linear Neural Dynamics
text: Motor Systems and Linear Neural Dynamics Brain-body-environment → feedback control → recurrent rate network → eigendecomposition → mode dynamics → effective time constant Draw the brain, body, and environment as a closed-loop dynamical system and distinguish feedforward commands, sensory feedback, state estimates, and external disturbances. Generalize the first-order equation for one neuron to \(\tau dh/dt=-h+Wh+I\), correctly interpreting the direction of \(W_{ij}\) and every matrix shape. When W is diagonalizable, transform population activity into its eigenbasis and derive mutually decoupled mode equations step by step. From eigenvalue \(\lambda _{i}\), derive effective time constant \(\tau /(1-\lambda _{i})\) and interpret \(\lambda _{i}<1\), =1, and >1 as decay, integration, and instability. Find the fixed point under constant input and distinguish long memory near an integrator, a perfect integrator, and runaway positive feedback. Motor control consists of closed-loop dynamics among brain, body, and environment, and neural activity is highly distributed. In a linear recurrent network, transforming individual neuronal activities into eigenmode coordinates decouples the system so each mode behaves like an independent first-order process. Eigenvalue \(\lambda\) sets effective time constant \(\tau /(1-\lambda )\): \(\lambda <1\) decays, \(\lambda \approx 1\) has long memory, \(\lambda =1\) is a perfect integrator, and \(\lambda >1\) grows without bound. Restricting a motor signal to one region and overlooking distributed population activity. Confusing neuronal activity coordinates with eigenmode coordinates. Treating an eigenmode as one neuron. Writing \(V^{-1}WV=D\) without checking the convention that columns of V are right eigenvectors. Using \(\tau /(1-\lambda )\) as a positive decay time when \(\lambda >1\). Assuming \(\lambda =1\) is automatically robust, despite its sensitivity to perturbation. Analyzing neural dynamics without body and environmental feedback. Distinguish individual-neuron activity, population-mode coordinates, and behavioral state; do not turn an eigenmode into one “special neuron.” Linear recurrent rate network \(\tau \) \(\dot{h} = -h + W h + I\) Common \(\tau\) and linearization Diagonalization \(W = V DV -1\) Diagonalizable W Mode coordinates \(\alpha  = V -1 h\) Invertible V Decoupled mode \(\tau \) \(\dot{\alpha }i = -(1 - \lambda _{i} )\alpha _{i} + \beta _{i}\) Eigenbasis Mode time constant \(\tau ef\) \(f = \tau  /(1 - \lambda )\) \(\lambda <1\) for stable decay Perfect integrator \(\lambda  = 1 \Rightarrow  \dot{\alpha } = \beta /\tau \) Exact cancellation of feedback and leak feedforward control Control based mainly on a prior model or command rather than current feedback correction. feedback control Online correction of action from sensory or state error. proprioception Sensory feedback about body position or force. recurrent network A network with feedback loops among its units. eigenmode A population activity pattern associated with an eigenvector of W. change of basis Conversion of the same state between neuronal and modal coordinates. effective time constant A mode's decay or integration timescale after feedback. fixed point A state whose derivative is zero. stability Whether a small perturbation returns to a fixed point. perfect integrator A mode that accumulates input without leak. Why does larger proportional gain improve disturbance rejection in a delay-free model but not justify infinite gain in a biological system? The ideal equation omits sensory delay, muscle dynamics, noise, saturation, and energetic cost. High gain amplifies noise and can cause overshoot or oscillation in a delayed loop, so stability must be assessed for the complete loop. Embed the motor system in coupled brain, body, and environment dynamics. Descending pathways change muscle activation; body mechanics convert activation into posture and velocity; gravity, contact, and object reaction forces alter body state; and proprioceptive, visual, and cutaneous signals return the outcome to the nervous system. Every arrow has delay and dynamics. Movement is therefore a time-evolving closed loop, not a static stimulus-response lookup. For asymmetric W, why can normalized right eigenvectors not justify writing \(\alpha =V^\mathrm{T} h\)? Right eigenvectors of an asymmetric matrix are generally not orthogonal, so \(V^\mathrm{T}V\ne I\). The correct transform is \(\alpha =V^{-1}h\), equivalently using the associated left eigenvectors to read amplitudes. Use right eigenvectors of W. If \(Wv_{i}=\lambda _{i} v_{i}\), multiplication by W rescales pattern \(v_{i}\) by \(\lambda _{i}\) without rotating it. Put these eigenvectors in the columns of V. If they are linearly independent, \(W=V\Lambda V^{-1}\). Expand activity as \(h=V\alpha\), where \(\alpha _{i}\) is the amplitude of population pattern i. This basis change leaves the physical state unchanged, just as a two-dimensional displacement can be expressed in oblique rather than x-y coordinates. Why does changing \(\lambda\) from 0.98 to 0.999 create drift risk in addition to longer memory? The denominator \(1-\lambda\) shrinks from 0.02 to 0.001, multiplying timescale and constant-input gain by twenty. A tiny persistent bias, low-frequency noise, or connectivity error produces a much larger state displacement. This also separates fixed point from timescale. For constant transformed input Ĩ_i and \(\lambda _{i}\ne 1\), \(\alpha _{i}*=\widetilde I_{i}/(1-\lambda _{i})\). The same small denominator creates both long \(\tau _{\mathrm{eff}}\) and high steady-state gain, so near-integration amplifies constant bias and parameter error. Memory is the benefit and drift the risk. Negative feedback, multiple timescales, and nonlinear bounds can manage that sensitivity. Which interpretation is supported by the schematic “In the Eigenbasis, Coupled Neuronal Dynamics Decompose into Independent Modes”? If recurrent matrix W is diagonalizable as \(W=V\Lambda V^{-1}\), activity \(h=V\alpha\) expresses a neuronal-space pattern in eigenmode amplitudes. After left multiplication by \(V^{-1}\), each \(\alpha _{i}\) independently obeys \(\tau \dot{\alpha }_i=-(1-\lambda _{i})\alpha _{i}+\widetilde I_{i}\). Thus \(\lambda _{i}\), rather than one neuron, sets decay, integration, or growth of that population pattern. A basis change is a mathematical coordinate transformation; a mode is not an anatomical neuron.

title: Lecture 19: Population Activity and Principal Component Analysis
subtitle: Population Activity and Principal Component Analysis
text: Population Activity and Principal Component Analysis two-neuron W → common/difference modes → mode regimes → activity-space trajectory → covariance → PCA top-K Starting from the two-neuron recurrent equation, compute by hand the eigenvalues, normalized eigenvectors, and input coordinates of the common and difference modes. Use each mode's time constant to classify stable decay, leaky integration, perfect integration, and unstable growth, then reinterpret the mode coordinates as trajectories in neural activity space. Derive PCA by maximizing the projection variance of centered data, and work through numerical examples of top-K projection, reconstruction, variance explained, and dimensional truncation. Distinguish rigorously between dynamical modes of a recurrent weight matrix and principal components of a covariance matrix, including when they may align and when no such alignment should be expected. Compare eigenvalue-cliff, cumulative-variance, and held-out-performance criteria for choosing dimensionality. The common and difference eigenmodes of a symmetric two-neuron network can be calculated completely by hand: one receives feedback +w0 and the other −w0. If the difference mode decays rapidly, the neural trajectory collapses toward the common-mode line and becomes approximately one-dimensional. PCA does not require W; it finds maximum projected variance from centered activity covariance. Dynamical eigenvectors of W can relate to principal components of C, but they are not generally identical. Equating eigenvectors of W with covariance PCs without additional assumptions. Omitting \(1/\sqrt 2\) when normalizing the common and difference modes. Using the wrong ± sign in the mode time constants. Misreading a low-dimensional trajectory as activity in only a few neurons. Applying PCA without centering the data. Treating maximum variance as maximum causal or behavioral relevance. Treating the eigenvalue cliff as an objectively unique dimensionality cutoff. PCA orders directions by variance; it does not automatically discover causal dynamics and can mix signal, noise, and condition structure. common and difference modes \(\xi \pm  = (1, \pm 1)T / 2\) symmetric two-neuron W orthonormal mode coordinates \(\alpha  = V\) Th \(V^\mathrm{T}V=I\) mode time constants \(\tau \pm  = \tau  /(1 \mp  w_{0} )\) \(|w_{0}|<1\) for stability of both modes activity covariance \(C = E[\delta h\delta hT ]\) centered data PC1 v1 = arg \(\max v\) T Cv \(\Vert v\Vert =1 C\) symmetric positive semidefinite PC score and projection pk = vkT \((h - \bar{h})\) orthonormal PCs cumulative variance explained ∑ ∑ VarFrac\((K) = \lambda _{k} / \lambda _{j} k\le K j\) sorted eigenvalues common mode An eigenmode in which both neurons change in the same direction. difference mode An eigenmode in which the two neurons change in opposite directions. neural activity space A state space whose coordinates are the activities of individual neurons. mode space A state space whose coordinates are dynamical eigenmode amplitudes. principal component analysis, PCA A linear method that orders orthogonal directions by the covariance variance they capture. principal component A covariance eigenvector together with the score obtained by projecting data onto it. projection The component of a vector along a specified basis direction. reconstruction An approximation of the original data formed from retained components. scree plot A plot of eigenvalue against component index. variance explained The fraction of the total eigenvalue sum retained by selected components. If \(I_{1}=1\) and \(I_{2}=-1\), which mode is driven directly? \(\beta _{+}=(1-1)/\sqrt 2=0\) and \(\beta _{-}=(1-(-1))/\sqrt 2=\sqrt 2\), so only the difference mode is driven directly; the neurons tend to change in opposite directions. Consider \(W=[[0,w_{0}],[w_{0},0]]\) with rate equations \(\tau dh_{1}/dt=-h_{1}+w_{0}h_{2}+I_{1}\) and \(\tau dh_{2}/dt=-h_{2}+w_{0}h_{1}+I_{2}\). Zeros on the diagonal mean that this teaching example has no self-coupling, while equal off-diagonal entries make the reciprocal coupling symmetric. That symmetry suggests testing \(h_{1}=h_{2}\) and \(h_{1}=-h_{2}\): exchanging the neurons leaves the first pattern unchanged and changes only the sign of the second. At \(w_{0}=-0.9\), which mode is slowest, and what is its time constant in units of \(\tau\)? The difference mode is slowest because \(\tau _{-}=\tau /(1-0.9)=10\tau\); the common mode has \(\tau _{+}=\tau /(1+0.9)\approx 0.526\tau\). Negative coupling near -1 preserves the opposing-change pattern. When \(|w_{0}|<1\), both 1-w0 and 1+w0 are positive, so both modes decay exponentially after input removal. As w0 approaches 1, \(\tau _{+}\) becomes long and the common coordinate behaves as a leaky integrator. At \(w_{0}=1\) the common equation has no leak: sustained input is integrated and the accumulated \(\alpha _{+}\) remains after the input ends. The same logic moves to the difference mode as w0 approaches -1. Equality marks a perfect integrator and should not be lumped into the ordinary leaky regime. If a constant input \(\beta _{-}=1\) acts at every moment, must \(\alpha _{-}\) approach zero? No. A stable difference mode approaches the nonzero fixed point \(\alpha _{-}* = \beta _{-}/(1+w_{0})\), so the trajectory can remain away from the common axis. Low-dimensional conclusions depend on input structure. Approximation quality can be measured by residual energy. Because the basis is orthonormal, \(||h||^{2}=\alpha +^{2}+\alpha -^{2}\). Discarding the difference mode gives squared reconstruction error exactly \(\alpha -^{2}\). An analyst may set a tolerance, for example calling the state 95% common-mode when \(\alpha -^{2}/(\alpha +^{2}+\alpha -^{2})<0.05\). This criterion is chosen for the analysis; it is not an absolute boundary that appears automatically in a sketch. What is chiefly mixed in if \(E[hh^\mathrm{T}]\) is computed without centering? The mean outer-product term \(\bar{h}\) \(\bar{h}^\mathrm{T}\) is included, so the leading direction may represent the mean firing pattern rather than trial or temporal fluctuations. Modes of W and PCs of C align only under additional conditions. For example, in a linear network driven by isotropic noise at stationarity, with W normal or symmetric, slow dynamical modes often accumulate more variance. Structured input, unequal noise, trial conditions, and nonlinear observations can all rotate the covariance. Similar axes motivate a hypothesis; statistical collinearity does not identify recurrent weights by itself. Why does \(V_{K}^\mathrm{T}V_{K}=I\) not imply \(V_{\mathrm{KV},K}^\mathrm{T}=I\)? When \(K<N\), \(V_{K}\) is not square. \(V_{K}^\mathrm{T}V_{K}\) is the identity in K-space, while \(V_{\mathrm{KV},K}^\mathrm{T}\) is the N-space projector onto a K-dimensional subspace. Order the covariance eigenvalues \(\lambda _{1}\ge \lambda _{2}\ge \cdots \ge \lambda _{N}\) with orthonormal eigenvectors v1,...,vN. PC one uses v1. PC two must be orthogonal to v1 and maximize variance in the remaining subspace, so it uses v2. Continuing gives \(V_{K}=[v_{1},\cdots,vK]\), an N×K matrix. For one centered sample, score vector \(p=V_{K}^\mathrm{T}(h-\bar{h})\) has K coordinates. Why does '95% variance explained' not guarantee retention of 95% of behavioral information? Variance measures activity amplitude, whereas behavioral information depends on condition distributions and the decoder. A low-variance direction may reliably distinguish choices, so the two percentages are not generally equivalent. Cumulative variance explained \(F(K)=\sum _{k=1}^K\lambda _{k}/\sum _{j=1}^N\lambda _{j}\) increases monotonically from \(F(0)=0\) to \(F(N)=1\). Its numerator must be \(\sum _{j=1}^K\lambda _{j}\) and its denominator the total variance \(\sum _{j=1}^N\lambda _{j}\); writing only \(\lambda _{i}\) or omitting the denominator no longer represents cumulative explained variance. Thresholds of 80%, 90%, or 95% give reproducible rules but need not be optimal for a particular scientific question. Measurement noise can raise the tail, condition means can create large PCs, and trial averaging can change the spectrum. Report preprocessing and the selection criterion together with K. Which interpretation is supported by the schematic “Scree-plot cliff and cumulative variance”? Read the two curves in principal-component order: beyond the cliff, each eigenvalue contributes little additional variance, while cumulative variance continues to rise monotonically. The elbow suggests candidate dimensionalities but does not determine a unique cutoff; the plotted coordinates illustrate the normalized relation and are not empirical data.

title: Lecture 20: Central Pattern Generators and Oscillations
subtitle: Central Pattern Generators and Oscillations
text: Central Pattern Generators and Oscillations pacemaker vs follower → half-center → complex eigenvalues → Morris–Lecar → nullclines/limit cycle → release vs escape Use synaptic-block logic to distinguish a cell-intrinsic pacemaker, a follower, and a network-generated half-center rhythm, while stating the limits of this experimental diagnosis. Solve for the complex eigenvalues of a two-neuron rotation matrix, using the real and imaginary parts to assess envelope stability and oscillation frequency, respectively. Explain every term in the Morris–Lecar voltage and recovery equations, then reconstruct the relaxation cycle from nullclines, fixed points, and fast–slow separation. Distinguish intrinsic release from intrinsic escape in a reciprocally inhibitory half-center, identifying whose intrinsic transition triggers each phase switch. Transfer the phase-plane geometry of a conductance model to a firing-rate model with adaptation while respecting the difference in model level. Whether rhythm persists after synaptic block can distinguish candidate intrinsic-pacemaker and network-generated mechanisms. Complex eigenvalues in a linear two-neuron system produce only damped or growing oscillatory components; a stable autonomous limit cycle requires nonlinearity. Fast voltage and slow recovery nullclines in Morris–Lecar generate a relaxation oscillation, while a mutually inhibitory half-center can alternate through intrinsic release or escape. Calling every rhythmic activity pattern a CPG. Assuming complex eigenvalues automatically imply sustained oscillation. Ignoring the real part of the full eigenvalue. Treating a nullcline as a trajectory. Assuming a fixed point is stable merely because a nullcline intersection exists. Distinguishing release from escape by superficial firing order rather than the intrinsic transition that triggers the switch. Excluding sensory feedback from real locomotor rhythms. Avoid classifying all rhythmic activity as a CPG, and do not conflate a damped linear oscillation with an autonomous nonlinear oscillator. complex mode \(\lambda  = a \pm  ib\) a controls the envelope; b controls frequency Euler decomposition e(a+ib)t = eat (cos bt + i sin bt) complex representation two-dimensional conductance model \(\dot{V} = F (V, N )\), \(\dot{N} = G(V, N )\) fast–slow variables V-nullcline \(F (V, N ) = 0\) \(dV/dt=0\) N-nullcline \(G(V, N ) = 0\) \(dN/dt=0\) sharp synaptic-threshold approximation \(S_{\infty } (V ) = H(V - VT )\) idealized switch central pattern generator, CPG A neural circuit that can generate a rhythmic motor pattern without periodic sensory drive. pacemaker neuron A neuron that oscillates spontaneously through intrinsic dynamics. half-center oscillator A network oscillator in which two mutually inhibitory units alternate activity. complex eigenvalue An eigenvalue that encodes both an exponential envelope and oscillatory phase. Morris-Lecar model A reduced, conductance-based neuron model with two variables. phase plane The trajectories and nullclines in a two-dimensional state space. relaxation oscillation A limit cycle that alternates slow drift with fast jumps. intrinsic release Removal of inhibition when the active neuron terminates its activity. intrinsic escape A transition in which the inhibited neuron recovers first and escapes inhibition. limit cycle A closed periodic orbit that attracts nearby trajectories. If both cells stop alternating after the block but continue to oscillate at different frequencies, is this a purely network-generated rhythm? No. Coordinated alternation depends on network coupling, but each cell retains intrinsic oscillatory capacity; the full mechanism is coupled intrinsic oscillators. Distinguish two origins of rhythmic activity. A cell-intrinsic pacemaker continues to generate a rhythm from its own voltage-gated currents even without periodic synaptic input; a follower does not oscillate on its own and simply tracks synaptic drive from a pacemaker. A network-generated rhythm is different: individual cells may remain tonic or silent in isolation, but reciprocal inhibition makes the pair alternate activity as a half-center oscillator. Respiration and alternating muscles during walking are useful functional examples. What happens if the full eigenvalues are \(0.2\pm 5i s^{-1}\)? The trajectory rotates while its envelope grows as \(e^{0.2t}\), producing an outward spiral. The linear model is unstable; whether a limit cycle subsequently forms depends on nonlinear saturation. The characteristic polynomial \(\det(W-\lambda I)=\lambda ^{2}+w_{0}^{2}=0\) gives λ_W=±i|w0|. A complex-mode solution contains \(e^{(-1\pm iw0)t/\tau }=e^{-t/\tau }[\cos(|w_{0}|t/\tau )\pm i \sin(|w_{0}|t/\tau )]\). Combining the conjugate pair yields real sine–cosine trajectories for h1 and h2. The angular frequency is \(\omega =|w_{0}|/\tau \mathrm{rad}/s\), and the ordinary frequency is \(f=\omega /(2\pi )\). Why is a nullcline not the neuron's actual trajectory? A nullcline is only the set of points where one derivative is instantaneously zero. The other variable usually continues to change, so the state crosses or moves nearby; only an intersection of both nullclines can remain stationary. Read a phase plane by determining signs in each region. Whether \(dV/dt\) is positive on a given side of the V-nullcline must be checked with a test point, not guessed from the curve's appearance. Below the N-nullcline, usually \(N<N_{\infty }\) and arrows point upward; above it, arrows point downward. A fixed point is stable if nearby arrows converge, a saddle if one direction converges and another diverges, and unstable if the flow departs overall. Why can two mutually inhibitory cells generate a network rhythm even when neither oscillates in isolation? Inhibition switches each partner's effective nullcline between active and inactive conditions. Slow recovery makes the cells reach their transitions in turn, so coupling creates periodic state switching. Even if the fixed point of each isolated cell is stable, mutual inhibition plus recovery can make the pair oscillate; conversely, not every mutually inhibitory pair oscillates. The system needs an intrinsic variable that evolves slowly in active and inhibited phases, a suitable synaptic threshold, and the right ordering of transitions. A sensory pulse can push one cell across a separatrix and reset phase without generating the rhythm itself. If the active cell falls below VT and its partner jumps 20 ms later, does that delay refute release? No. Release requires only that removal of inhibition be the upstream trigger. The partner still takes finite time to leave its low state according to its own membrane and recovery dynamics. Approximate the synapse with a sharp threshold: \(S_{\infty }(V)=0\) when \(V<VT\) and 1 when \(V>VT\). While the active cell's V exceeds VT, it inhibits its partner; once V falls below VT, inhibition shuts off rapidly. A free neuron follows the \(F(V,N)=0\) nullcline, whereas an inhibited neuron follows a shifted nullcline that includes synaptic current. Switching between these two geometries makes the identity of the first threshold-crosser an observable mechanistic criterion. Why are two linear rate variables h1 and h2 usually insufficient for a stable half-center limit cycle? A linear system can only decay, rotate neutrally, or grow; it lacks a slow state and amplitude regulation. Adaptation or recovery plus nonlinear F supplies phase switching and a bounded cycle. While cell i is active, high \(h_{i}\) slowly raises \(a_{i}\). Increasing adaptation lowers effective drive until the active rate falls. Inhibition of the partner then weakens, allowing it to rise and subsequently inhibit the original cell. This is release-like switching. If \(a_{j}\) falls during the inhibited cell's low-activity phase, restoring its effective excitability until it crosses threshold first, switching is escape-like. Which interpretation is supported by the schematic “Morris–Lecar nullclines and the relaxation cycle”? The intersection of the two nullclines is a candidate equilibrium. Here it is unstable, so the trajectory moves slowly along the outer attracting branches of the V-nullcline and jumps rapidly to the other branch near each fold. Long portions of the loop represent slow recovery, whereas nearly horizontal crossings represent fast voltage transitions. The curves are a normalized schematic of the mechanisms.

title: Lecture 21: Oculomotor Integrator, Degeneracy, and Sloppy Models
subtitle: Oculomotor Integrator, Degeneracy, and Sloppy Models
text: Oculomotor Integrator, Degeneracy, and Sloppy Models velocity→position → bilateral integrator → dominant \(\lambda =1\)→ weight-family degeneracy → nonlinear synapse fit → least squares/Hessian Explain why integrating an eye-velocity command requires a persistent neural state after a saccade, and connect bilateral excitation/inhibition to left–right position tuning. Derive the characteristic equation, eigenvalue-one constraint, and compensating weight family for a general \(2\times 2\) recurrent matrix, while also checking transverse stability. Use the inverse of a measured F–I curve and fixed synaptic nonlinearities to construct a design matrix, turning an apparently nonlinear circuit fit into row-wise least squares. Use the eigendecomposition of a quadratic loss Hessian to explain stiff and sloppy directions, parameter compensation, and an ensemble of adequate models. Distinguish low dimensionality in neural-state space, sloppiness in parameter space, measurement uncertainty, and genuine biological degeneracy. The oculomotor integrator must retain eye position after a saccade, so the network needs a long-time-scale mode near \(\lambda =1\). For a general \(2\times 2\) W, perfect integration imposes only \(\det(I-W)=0\), leaving a many-to-one family of weights; parameter degeneracy is still stronger in complex biological models. Once measured tuning and synaptic nonlinearities are fixed, fitting can be rewritten as linear regression. Hessian eigenvalues separate a few stiff combinations from many sloppy ones, motivating an adequate-model ensemble rather than a unique best fit. Mistaking persistent eye position for a sensory afterimage rather than an integral of velocity. Requiring \(\lambda =1\) but failing to check stability of the other modes. Using the division-based family formula even when \(W_{12}=0\). Treating a many-to-one parameter mapping as measurement noise. Confusing low dimensionality in neural-state space with sloppiness in parameter space. Interpreting a sloppy parameter as biologically irrelevant. Reporting only best-fit weights without uncertainty or an ensemble. Low dimensionality in neural-state space and sloppiness in parameter space must be distinguished; they are different ideas in different spaces. eye-position integration Z t \(x(t) = x(0) + v(t' )dt'\) 0 velocity command eigenvalue 1 condition \(\det(I - W ) = 0\) perfect linear integrator weight-compensation family \(W_{21} = (1 - W_{11} )(1 - W_{22} )/W_{12}\) \(W_{12}\ne 0\) row-wise OLS fit \(\hat{W} = Y X T\) (XX T )−1 \(XX^\mathrm{T}\) invertible Hessian eigendecomposition \(H = V DV T H\) symmetric local parameter sensitivity 1X ∆\(L = \lambda _{k}\) zk2 2 quadratic approximation oculomotor integrator A circuit that converts an eye-velocity command into a persistent eye-position signal. line attractor A continuous family of nearly stable states capable of storing a graded value. parameter degeneracy The ability of different parameter combinations to produce similar output or function. identifiability The extent to which data uniquely or sufficiently constrain parameters. Hessian The local curvature matrix of loss with respect to parameters. stiff direction A parameter combination to whose variation the loss is highly sensitive. sloppy direction A parameter combination to whose variation the loss is insensitive. model ensemble A set of parameterizations that all explain the data adequately. parameter compensation Offsetting a change in one parameter with changes in others. If position returns to center after the velocity command with a time constant of 5 s, is this still an integrator? It is a leaky rather than perfect integrator. Behavior may appear persistent for periods shorter than 5 s, but a long delay reveals measurable drift. Moving the eye requires phasic motor drive to generate velocity and tonic drive to oppose orbital restoring forces and hold the new position. The course abstracts the distributed brainstem and cerebellar network as a neural integrator: its input is the eye-velocity command \(v(t)\), and its output state approximates \(x(t)=x(0)+\int v(t')dt'\). Ideally, x retains its latest value when v returns to zero; if the network leaks, position slowly drifts back toward center. What happens if the same constraint gives \(\lambda _{2}=1.1\)? The memory mode still has \(\lambda =1\), but the transverse mode's full growth rate is \((1.1-1)/\tau >0\). Any small error grows, so the full network is not a stable, usable integrator. Expanding gives \(\det(I-W)=(1-W_{11})(1-W_{22})-W_{12}W_{21}=0\). If \(W_{12}\ne 0\), solve \(W_{21}=(1-W_{11})(1-W_{22})/W_{12}\). Once three weights are chosen, the fourth compensates; increasing a self-weight can be offset by changing cross-coupling while preserving \(\lambda =1\). This is a many-to-one functional mapping: different parameter points share the same integrator eigenvalue. Why does fitting become linear after fixing the nonlinearities even though the neuron response itself remains nonlinear? \(S_{j}\) and \(F_{i}^{-1}\) already apply nonlinear transformations to the data. Only the unknown weights linearly combine those transformed features; the full input–output mapping remains nonlinear. With the nonlinear functions fixed, the prediction is \(\hat{Y}_{i\mu }=\sum _j W_{ij} X_{j}\mu\), linear in the unknown weights Wij and bias. Each output neuron i can fit one row of weights independently. If M sample positions are columns, X has shape D×M, Y is N×M, W is N×D, and \(\hat{Y}=WX\) is dimensionally consistent. State this orientation explicitly, because placing samples in rows yields a transposed formula. How does adding a ridge penalty \(\lambda ||w||^{2}/2\) change the Hessian? H becomes \(XX^\mathrm{T}+\lambda I\). Every eigenvalue increases by \(\lambda\), stabilizing the inverse, but the estimate is biased toward zero; regularization must not be mistaken for additional data. This connects fitting with experimental design. If one feature combination barely changes across positions, X contains little information along that direction and H has a small eigenvalue. Conditions that selectively activate that combination can increase curvature and tighten parameter uncertainty. Sloppiness need not be accepted passively; perturbations and improved sampling can reduce it. Why can sloppy not be translated as 'this parameter is unimportant'? A Hessian direction usually combines parameters, and small curvature means only that the current data and loss are insensitive to it. The combination may still be crucial for an unmeasured behavior, a perturbation response, or biological viability. A Hessian is symmetric positive-semidefinite, so \(H=VDV^\mathrm{T}\), where columns \(v_{k}\) are orthonormal parameter directions and D contains \(\lambda _{k}\ge 0\). Let \(z=V^\mathrm{T}(w-\hat{w})\); then the quadratic loss increase is \(\Delta L=1/2\sum \lambda _{k} z_{k}^{2}\). A large \(\lambda _{k}\) gives a large loss for the same displacement and defines a stiff direction. A small \(\lambda _{k}\) permits farther movement within the adequate-fit contour and defines a sloppy direction. Which interpretation is supported by the schematic “Three fates of an eigenvalue-one integrator”? After input is removed, the fate of the same initial mode amplitude depends only on \(1-\lambda\): when \(\lambda <1\) it leaks; when \(\lambda =1\) the restoring coefficient in the derivative vanishes and memory persists; when \(\lambda >1 a\) small deviation grows. Thus \(\det(I-W)=0\) guarantees only an integrating mode, and the stability of all remaining modes must still be checked.

title: Lecture 22: Motor Cortex Latent Dynamics and Brain–Machine Interfaces
subtitle: Motor Cortex Latent Dynamics and Brain–Machine Interfaces
text: Motor Cortex Latent Dynamics and Brain–Machine Interfaces center-out tuning → PCA low dimension → latent vs activity space → GPFA → preparatory trajectories → output-null readout Distinguish three levels of description—single-neuron directional tuning, low-dimensional population trajectories, and latent dynamics—and explain how all three can hold simultaneously. Explain each component of GPFA from high-dimensional neural activity to low-dimensional factors, including the observation model, temporal covariance, matrix shapes, and non-identifiability. Use a delayed-reach timeline to explain how preparatory states enter movement-potent and output-null subspaces without misrepresenting graphical correlations as causal conclusions. Compute the null space and rank–nullity of a linear readout by hand, construct a simple decoder, and apply the results to closed-loop BMI and cross-day alignment. Connect PCA/GPFA, linear readout, closed-loop feedback, and cross-day alignment into a testable BMI analysis pipeline. Directional tuning is a classic description of motor cortex, whereas the modern population view asks whether low-dimensional trajectories generate movement dynamics. GPFA embeds smooth latent factors into noisy neural activity with a Gaussian observation model and explicitly models temporal covariance. A preparatory state can vary within the null space of muscle readout U without causing movement. BMI decodes neural or latent state into device commands and uses feedback and cross-day latent alignment to improve stability. Conflating a single-neuron tuning curve with a latent trajectory. Using PCA components, GPFA factors, dynamical modes, and decoder axes interchangeably. Assuming that a K-dimensional model means only K neurons matter. Ignoring non-identifiability of \(C-\alpha\) scale and rotation. Inferring \(r=0\) from \(Ur=0\). Ignoring user feedback and learning in a feedforward BMI account. Describing cross-day latent stability as absolute invariance. Tuning curves, principal components, latent factors, dynamical modes, and decoder axes must be distinguished explicitly. They may be related, but they are not interchangeable. GPFA observation model rt |αt ∼ N (Cαt + d, Σ) Gaussian approximation GP temporal covariance ′ 2 \(K(t, t' ) = \sigma s_{2} e-(t-t ) /(2\tau  ) + \sigma n_{2} \delta tt'\) 2 stationary smooth kernel linear motor readout \(m = Ur\) local approximation output-null space Null(U ) = {r: U r = 0} linear algebra rank–nullity dim N ull\((U ) = N - \operatorname{rank}(U )\) U: M×N latent decoder \(\hat{v} = B\alpha \) aligned latent coordinates center-out reach task A reaching paradigm from a central location to multiple radial targets. direction tuning Variation of the mean response with reach direction. latent factor A low-dimensional hidden variable that explains shared population variability. embedding A mapping from latent coordinates into high-dimensional activity. Gaussian-process factor analysis, GPFA A latent-factor model with a temporal Gaussian-process prior. preparatory activity A target-dependent population state before movement. output-null space Neural directions that do not change the current readout. output-potent space Directions that change muscle or device output. brain-machine interface, BMI A system that controls an external device from neural activity. closed-loop control Online control that includes sensory or device feedback. Why does a PC explaining 70% of neural variance not necessarily explain 70% of behavioral variance? Behavior depends on a separate readout map, which may ignore high-variance directions or amplify low-variance directions; there is no fixed ratio between the two variances. A center-out task begins at a central location and reaches toward multiple radial targets, making direction, speed, and time from the go cue well structured. For one neuron, mean directional tuning can be described by \(r(\theta )=b+k \cos(\theta -\theta _{\mathrm{pref}})\), where \(\theta _{\mathrm{pref}}\) is preferred direction and k is modulation depth. This formula summarizes a condition average; it does not mean the neuron 'knows' the angle or guarantee that other movement variables have been excluded. If one latent factor is multiplied everywhere by 2 without changing C, is it still the same GPFA model? No; the predicted mean changes. It is an equivalent coordinate reparameterization only if the corresponding column of C is also divided by 2. A K-dimensional trajectory in latent space is embedded by C into N-dimensional activity space. The column span of C is the shared-activity subspace allowed by the model, while \(\Sigma\) usually absorbs neuron-specific residuals. Shared variation does not require neuron pairs to have identical waveforms: positive and negative loadings allow one factor to produce different amplitudes and directions across cells. Why does a smooth kernel not prove that the true cortical trajectory is intrinsically smooth? Some smoothness comes from the prior. Compare held-out data, alternative kernels, and temporal resolutions to determine whether the data support that time scale. Read a delayed-reach plot along its timeline. The interval after target onset but before the go cue is the preparatory epoch; movement begins only after go. Preparatory activity for different targets may approach different latent locations without producing obvious movement. After the cue, trajectories depart from those initial states along target-specific movement paths. The plot supports the idea that an initial condition influences later dynamics, but trajectories alone cannot exclude sustained common input. If the downstream readout changes to \(U'\), must the original output-null vector remain null? No. The null space depends on the particular readout. One neural direction may be irrelevant to one output yet affect another muscle group or cognitive variable. Output-null does not mean computation-null. Activity along a null direction can set a recurrent initial condition, suppress an erroneous movement, or prepare multiple candidates. The same neural vector may also affect unrecorded downstream populations. The course diagram is a linear framework that separates the existence of activity from the existence of current output; it does not justify calling null activity biologically functionless. Why can an improvement in closed-loop performance not be attributed entirely to more accurate decoder parameters? The participant changes neural strategy in response to feedback, and the decoder may update online. Performance comes from joint adaptation, so one side must be frozen or otherwise controlled to separate the causes. A BMI decoder maps neural features to cursor velocity, position, or a discrete action. During open-loop calibration, the participant observes prescribed movement or attempts an action while the system fits a mapping offline. In closed loop, decoder output immediately changes visual feedback, so participant and decoder coadapt. Closed-loop performance is therefore not a passive measure of a fixed encoding; the brain, decoder, and feedback form a new dynamical system. Which interpretation is supported by the schematic “From population activity to closed-loop BMI”? Observed activity is first compressed by GPFA into daily latent coordinates, then \(A_{d}\) aligns those coordinates to a shared space and passes them to shared decoder B. Decoder output changes cursor feedback, which in turn changes subsequent neural activity. Cross-day stability therefore means that a low-dimensional mapping is transferable; it does not require each neuron's loading to remain fixed.

title: Lecture 23: Short-Term Memory and Perceptual Decisions
subtitle: Short-Term Memory and Perceptual Decisions
text: Short-Term Memory and Perceptual Decisions cognition/decoupling → DMS/Romo → persistent activity → long recurrent mode → drift-diffusion → psychometric/chronometric/LIP Organize decision-making, working memory, and long-term learning around the working definition that current brain state is not determined solely by current input, while recognizing that this is not an exhaustive definition. Reconstruct DMS and Romo parametric working-memory tasks through sample, delay, comparison, and choice, specifying what information must be retained during the delay. Derive the effective time constant of graded persistent activity from a recurrent eigenmode and classify leaky, perfectly persistent, and unstable regimes. Explain the evidence, noise, bias, bounds, and reaction time of a leaky drift-diffusion process, and predict its psychometric and chronometric curves. Use the Wong–Wang phase plane to distinguish fixed points, separatrices, and stochastic choice while keeping model predictions separate from correlations in LIP. This lecture provisionally defines cognition as a brain state not determined solely by present input. Short-term memory can preserve a past sample in persistent population modes without immediately modifying synapses. Perceptual decisions can be described behaviorally by noisy evidence accumulation and bounds; LIP ramps are correlated neural variables, not automatic proof of mechanism. A reduced Wong–Wang attractor model uses two-dimensional nonlinear nullclines to connect integration, competition, and discrete choice. Treating the working definition of cognition as a complete philosophical or psychological definition. Assuming that STM requires immediate synaptic plasticity. Conflating persistent single-cell activity with a stable population mode. Treating the DDM decision variable as a directly observed neuron. Fitting only the psychometric function and not testing the chronometric function. Equating an LIP correlation directly with a causal accumulator. Conflating a descriptive DDM with a biophysical attractor model at the same explanatory level. Distinguish working-memory content, neural correlates, persistent modes, and synaptic memory; also distinguish a descriptive DDM from a biophysical attractor model. persistent memory mode \(\tau ef\) \(f = \tau  /(1 - \lambda )\) \(\lambda <1\) but close to 1 leaky evidence accumulator \(\tau a\) \(\dot{a} = -a + e(t) + \gamma (t)\) white or colored noise specified decision bias \(a(0) = b\) initial-condition interpretation absorbing decision bounds \(a = \pm B\) first-passage rule psychometric function \(P (\mathrm{choice}|c)\) signed stimulus strength chronometric function \(E[RT |c]\) state whether nondecision time is included Wong–Wang nullclines \(G_{1} = 0\), \(G_{2} = 0 2D\) reduced dynamics cognition This lecture's working definition: a brain state partly decoupled from present input and shaped by past events or future goals. short-term memory The ability to retain recently encountered information briefly. working memory Information retained for use in a current computation. delayed match-to-sample A sample–delay–test memory task. persistent activity Neural activity that remains after the stimulus ends. drift-diffusion model, DDM A decision model that accumulates noisy evidence to bounds. psychometric curve Choice or accuracy as a function of stimulus strength. chronometric curve Reaction time as a function of stimulus strength. separatrix A boundary separating different attractor basins. attractor A state or set toward which nearby states converge under the dynamics. Why does continued brain activity with the eyes closed not by itself prove cognition in this lecture's sense? Persistent activity may be spontaneous fluctuation or an unmeasured input. It must carry task-relevant history and predict later behavior. This lecture adopts a working definition: cognition makes brain state or behavior incompletely determined by present sensory input. The same current stimulus can produce different responses under different memories, goals, or beliefs; conversely, an internal decision variable can keep evolving while the outside world is unchanged. This definition is useful for modeling, but it is not a complete philosophical definition of consciousness, language, or intelligence. Why does monotonic delay-period firing with f1 not by itself prove that this is the memory used for behavior? The correlated signal could be a passive readout. Functional evidence is stronger when its trial fluctuations, selective perturbation, or downstream coupling affect comparison behavior. In the Romo vibration task, frequency f1 is delivered to a fingertip, followed after a delay by f2; the animal judges whether f2 is greater or less than f1. Comparing neighboring frequencies requires a graded magnitude, not merely a 'stimulus occurred' marker. If the delay representation is noisy, f1 and f2 become harder to discriminate as they approach each other, and psychometric slope can estimate their combined sensory and memory uncertainty. Why does increasing \(\lambda\) from 0.99 to 1.01 not simply lengthen memory a little? It crosses the stability boundary. The linear mode changes from slow decay to exponential growth and needs another nonlinearity to limit amplitude. Persistent activity of individual neurons may change over time while a population projection remains stable.
