Conversely, a condition-averaged cell may look flat because different trial dynamics cancel. Examine decoding across the delay, population trajectories, single-trial drift, and behavioral error together. Short-term memory need not alter synaptic weights online on every trial; the existing recurrent network state can store it. Why do identical coherence values yield different choices and RTs? Each trial has a different noise path, which changes both the first-passage time and which boundary is reached first. In simulation, update a with a small step \(\Delta t\) and stop at the first boundary crossing; do not average after crossing and then decide. Noise scaling must vary with the square root of \(\Delta t\). Adding a fixed-variance noise term each step makes the model change when the time step changes. Begin with deterministic constant evidence, then add randomness and observe how the distribution forms. Why can mean LIP ramp slopes alone not distinguish accumulation from averaged discrete steps? Both forms of single-trial dynamics can yield similar smooth curves when different onset or choice times are averaged, requiring single-trial model comparison. A psychometric function plots P(choice|signed coherence). Choice is nearly uncertain around zero coherence and saturates toward the correct option as coherence magnitude grows. Horizontal displacement suggests bias, while slope reflects overall sensitivity but also depends on sensory noise, integration, and lapses. An accuracy curve alone often cannot distinguish drift, bound, and noise. Why do two choice attractors generally require a saddle or basin boundary between them? Distinct basins of attraction in a continuous dynamical system must be separated by a boundary that flows to neither attractor. In two dimensions, that boundary is commonly the stable manifold of a saddle. Intersections of \(G_{1}=0\) and \(G_{2}=0\) are fixed points. Under absent or weak evidence, a common topology contains a low-activity undecided state, two choice attractors, and a saddle on the basin boundary. Other parameter settings produce other topologies, so the schematic is not a universal theorem. A separatrix through the saddle assigns initial states and noise paths to the two attractor basins. Which interpretation is supported by the schematic “First-passage paths in drift–diffusion”? Each path begins at bias b, accumulates noisy evidence step by step, and stops the first time it reaches +B or −B. The endpoint determines choice and the horizontal coordinate determines decision time. Under identical task parameters, noise can carry the two trajectories to different boundaries; a trajectory must not be averaged further after crossing before a decision is assigned.

title: Lecture 24: Learning from Rewards
subtitle: Learning from Rewards
text: Learning from Rewards stimulus/action/reward → three-factor plasticity → reward baseline/covariance → matching law → Rescorla–Wagner → TD/RPE Organize stimulus, action, reward, and synaptic eligibility into a three-factor learning rule, explaining why naive reward-gated Hebbian learning remains excessively strong. Derive the reward-baseline covariance update and matching equilibrium, stating assumptions such as stationary reward and the choice rule at each step. Derive Rescorla–Wagner learning from squared prediction error and use blocking to explain why an already predicted reward produces no further learning. Express delayed reward as a temporal-difference error and distinguish state value, action value, reward-prediction error, and dopamine response. Read dopamine timelines for early reward, cue transfer, and omission while preserving the evidential boundary for alternatives such as salience. Learned decisions must connect stimulus/action activity to delayed reward. A simple reward-gated Hebbian rule keeps strengthening when reward is common; subtracting the expected-reward baseline turns it into a covariance rule. Under a specified choice model and assumptions, the stationary covariance condition produces matching behavior. Rescorla–Wagner learns cue value from current reward-prediction error, while TD extends error to future value. Dopamine cue-transfer and omission patterns resemble RPE, though dopamine signals may also mix salience and movement. Failing to subtract a baseline from reward-gated Hebbian learning, so every rewarded coactivity continues to strengthen. Treating matching as an unconditional law of rational optimality. Explaining blocking by claiming that S2 did not coincide with reward. Conflating RPE, value, and salience. Omitting \(\gamma\) or next value from TD error. Treating dopamine as the only third factor in all reward learning. Prematurely treating this lecture's simplified Q concept as a complete Q-learning algorithm. Lecture 24 is a biological and reward-learning bridge; Lecture 25 introduces MDP/RL systematically. Do not let Bellman equations or Q-learning obscure this lecture's plasticity and dopamine logic. reward-baseline three-factor update ∆\(w = \eta e(R - \bar{R})\) eligibility e defined covariance learning E[∆w] = \(\eta \operatorname{Cov}(e, R)\) stationary average matching law \(CA /CB \approx  RA /RB\) specific foraging assumptions linear value predictor \(V = w_{\mathrm{T}} x\) features x Rescorla–Wagner update ∆\(w = \eta x(R - V )\) immediate or represented reward TD/RPE \(\delta  = R + \gamma V_{\mathrm{next}} - V\) Markov or state representation implicit state–action value \(Q(s, a) = E[G|s, a]\) policy and future behavior specified reward learning Adjustment of stimulus–action associations by outcomes. eligibility \(\operatorname{trace} A\) variable marking recent pre/post or action activity for modification by a later reward. reward baseline Expected reward used to compute a signal above or below expectation. matching law Approximate matching of choice proportions to obtained-reward proportions. value Expected discounted future reward from the current state or cue. Rescorla-Wagner rule A rule that updates cue value using reward-prediction error. blocking Failure of a new cue to learn because an existing predictor leaves zero error. temporal-difference error, TD error Reward plus discounted next value minus current value. reward-prediction error, RPE The difference between an actual or updated target and predicted value. Q value Expected return conditioned on a state–action pair. Why should a dopamine pulse without preceding eligibility not selectively strengthen one stimulus–action synapse? The third factor broadcasts the outcome, but local eligibility identifies the synapse that participated in the action; without eligibility, there is no correct credit address. A foraging animal selects an action from a sensory cue and receives reward. Learning must establish the stimulus–action–outcome relation rather than strengthen every recently active synapse. Let x be a presynaptic stimulus feature and y postsynaptic or action activity, so xy creates eligibility. A third factor M arrives after the outcome, giving update \(\Delta w=\eta Mxy\). An eligibility trace can bridge the delay from action to reward. Why does an underestimated baseline produce systematic positive drift? The mean of R-b becomes positive. If mean eligibility is also positive, an offset update appears that is unrelated to genuine reward–eligibility covariance. A baseline may be a global running average or depend on state or choice. A global baseline has lower variance but can be biased when reward scales differ across states. A state-dependent value baseline is more precise but requires additional parameters. For its expected conditional dependence to remain valid, the baseline must not improperly inspect the outcome of the current action. Why does a matching curve not prove that the animal explicitly computes RA/RB? A long-run ratio can emerge automatically from local prediction-error updates and stochastic choice; the behavioral equality does not uniquely identify the internal algorithm. The derivation assumes continued sampling of both sides, an approximately stationary reward schedule, comparable cost per choice, and negligible changeover delay, satiety, and risk sensitivity. When reward magnitudes differ, match obtained value rather than raw count. Undermatching, overmatching, and bias can be described by generalized matching: \(\log(CA/CB)=a \log(RA/RB)+\log b\). If reward is unchanged but the prediction from old cue A is removed, why does B begin learning again? The total prediction falls and positive prediction error returns. Because B is active, it now receives an update—the logic of unblocking. Rescorla–Wagner and TD both depend on feature representation. Blocking changes if A and B are highly similar or a hidden context shifts; zero error may also reflect reduced attention. A model account should state alternative mechanisms and distinguish them with unblocking, reward revaluation, and trial-level learning curves. Why does equal state value not imply that two actions are equally good? V is a policy-weighted average. One action may have high Q and another low Q while producing the same aggregate V under a particular policy. In a delayed task, expand a sustained cue into time-specific features x1,x2,… so the learner knows which interval follows the cue. TD updates begin with features near reward and propagate to earlier features across trials. One time-invariant feature cannot easily represent when reward will arrive or predict a negative error at omission time. Why does an omission dip support prediction error more strongly than merely observing no burst at reward time? It is a negative signal below baseline timed to the expected reward. A purely nonnegative reward detector cannot naturally generate this timed negative response. If predicted reward is omitted at its expected time, \(Rt+1=0\) and next value collapses, making \(\delta\) negative at that moment and producing a dip. Accurate dip timing requires a temporal representation of when reward should arrive; a one-state-per-trial model cannot place the negative error precisely. Together, the three timelines constrain a prediction-error account rather than a pure reward response. Which interpretation is supported by the schematic “TD error transfers from reward to a predictive cue”? Compare the same trial row by row. Before learning, only unexpected reward produces positive \(\delta\). After the cue–reward relation is learned, positive \(\delta\) moves earlier to the cue and is nearly zero when reward arrives on time. If reward is omitted at the deadline, negative \(\delta\) appears then. This pattern of signs supports prediction error rather than a pure reward response.

title: Lecture 25: Reinforcement Learning: MDPs, Bellman Equations, and Q-Learning
subtitle: Reinforcement Learning: MDPs, Bellman Equations, and Q-Learning
text: Reinforcement Learning: MDPs, Bellman Equations, and Q-Learning agent/state/action/reward → Markov property → discounted return → V/Q/policy → Bellman backup → Q-learning/exploration Define an MDP completely in terms of agent, state, action, reward, and a transition distribution, and use counterexamples to test whether a state satisfies the Markov property. Derive discounted return, \(V_{\pi }\), and \(Q_{\pi }\) from a reward sequence, computing both a finite chain and an infinite geometric series by hand. Derive the Bellman expectation and optimality equations by splitting return after its first step, making explicit that the maximum ranges over actions in the next state. Carry out tabular Q-learning and ε-greedy exploration update by update, distinguishing the behavior policy, target, and off-policy update. Compare model-free learning, model-based learning, generative representations, and replay while rigorously separating algorithmic variables from hippocampal evidence. The central MDP claim is not that the environment has no history, but that the chosen state representation makes the future conditionally independent of earlier history given current state and action. Discounted return decomposes recursively into immediate reward plus \(\gamma\) times future return, yielding the Bellman optimality equation. Q-learning uses a sampled Bellman error for an off-policy bootstrap update. Model-based RL also learns a transition/reward model and can improve sample efficiency with simulated experience or replay. Equating the Markov property with an environment that has no history. Confusing \(V_{\pi }\), \(Q_{\pi }\), \(V^{*}\), and \(Q^{*}\). Omitting the transition expectation from the Bellman equation. Using the behavior action in a Q-learning target and inadvertently writing SARSA. Assuming that the random branch of ε-greedy samples only nongreedy actions without stating that convention. Equating model-free learning with an absence of internal representation. Equating hippocampal replay directly with an exact Bellman backup. Q-learning is not a synonym for every TD-learning method, and hippocampal replay is not directly equivalent to an exact Bellman backup; evidence and inference must be distinguished explicitly. MDP transition/reward model \(p(s', r|s, a)\) Markov state discounted return Gt = \(\gamma \) k Rt+k+1 \(k\ge 0\) \(0\le \gamma <1\) or a finite episode state value \(V_{\pi } (s) = E_{\pi } [G_{t} |s_{t} = s]\) policy \(\pi\) state-action value \(Q_{\pi } (s, a) = E_{\pi } [G_{t} |s_{t} = s, a_{t} = a]\) first action fixed Bellman optimality \(Q\ast  = E[R + \gamma  \max Q\ast  ]\) optimal continuation tabular Q-learning Q ← Q + α(R + γ max Q′ − Q) sampled transition ε-greedy exploration \(\pi \epsilon  = (1 - \epsilon )\)greedy \(+ \epsilon \mathrm{random}\) finite action set reinforcement learning A framework that learns a policy or value through interaction and rewards. agent A learner that selects actions and updates an internal policy or model. state An environment representation used to predict the future and select an action. Markov property The conditional independence of the future from earlier history given the current state and action. policy A mapping from states to action probabilities. return The discounted sum of future rewards. Bellman equation A recursive self-consistency relation for value. Q-learning A model-free, off-policy TD control algorithm. exploration-exploitation The tradeoff between gathering new information and selecting the currently best action. model-based reinforcement learning A reinforcement-learning approach that learns or uses an environment model for planning. replay A neural or computational process that reinstates or simulates state sequences offline. Why might adding the trial number to state improve training prediction but still be a poor representation? It may memorize samples without capturing generalizable, future-relevant structure and will perform poorly in held-out contexts. An MDP is defined by states, actions, reward, and the transition–reward distribution \(p(s',r|s,a)\). The Markov property says that, conditioned on current s and a, the next outcome does not change with earlier trajectory. It does not require a deterministic environment: one s,a pair may lead randomly to several \(s'\) values, provided the probabilities are determined fully by current state. Why does a in \(Q_{\pi }(s,a)\) fix only the first step? The definition conditions on \(a_{t}=a\). Future actions are sampled from \(\pi\) beginning in the next state, so Q evaluates 'take a first, then follow \(\pi\).' \(V_{\pi }(s)=E_{\pi }[G_{t}|s_{t}=s]\) averages over environmental randomness and future policy actions. \(Q_{\pi }(s,a)=E_{\pi }[G_{t}|s_{t}=s,a_{t}=a]\) fixes only the first action, after which \(\pi\) is followed. Consequently, \(V_{\pi }(s)=\sum _{a}\pi (a|s)Q_{\pi }(s,a)\); under a deterministic policy, only the selected action contributes. Why can the maximum not be moved outside the expectation while fixing the same \(a'\)? Different random next states can have different best actions. Averaging first would force one action across states and change the optimal-continuation problem. The Bellman operator maps one Q table to another. In the tabular discounted setting with \(\gamma <1\) it is a contraction, so repeated backups approach a unique fixed point. As \(\gamma\) approaches 1, information reaches farther but contraction slows. Function approximation and off-policy sampling can invalidate this simple convergence guarantee. Why can the random branch of ε-greedy still select the greedy action? The random branch samples uniformly from all actions, including the greedy action, so total greedy probability exceeds \(1-\epsilon\). In behavioral analysis, exploration should not simply be labeled random error; animals may direct exploration toward uncertain actions. Fitting ε-greedy to systematic uncertainty seeking misattributes it to value or temperature. Model comparisons should include alternatives such as softmax and directed exploration. Why is immediate sensitivity to revaluation not sufficient proof of a complete internal map? Other rules, instructions, or direct cues can also alter choice rapidly; constrain the explanation with multiple novel transitions and control conditions. Tolman-style maze results suggest that animals can learn environmental structure rather than a single stimulus–response chain. When reward location changes or a familiar route closes, an agent with a transition map and reward model can plan before traversing every route again. A purely cached model-free Q estimate generally needs new prediction errors to change gradually. Why is more replay not always better? If the learned model has systematic error, repeated simulation amplifies its bias; coverage, priority, and model uncertainty must be balanced. Hippocampal replay reinstates place-cell sequences during rest or sleep. Sequences may run forward or backward, be temporally compressed, and favor reward or future paths. Replay is compatible with memory consolidation, planning, and credit propagation, but detecting a sequence does not show that downstream circuitry performs a particular numerical update; replay may serve several functions. Which interpretation is supported by the schematic “The agent–environment loop and a one-step Bellman backup”? In the forward interaction, policy maps \(s_{t}\) to \(a_{t}\), after which the environment samples r and \(s_{t+1}\). The backup then uses \(r+\gamma \max_{a'}Q(s_{t+1},a')\) to update current \(Q(s_{t},a_{t})\). A dashed path carries \(s_{t+1}\) into the next cycle, showing that the Markov transition and value backup are connected steps pointing in opposite directions.

title: Lecture 26: Hopfield Associative Memory
subtitle: Hopfield Associative Memory
text: Hopfield Associative Memory Hebbian assembly → binary asynchronous dynamics → energy → stored attractors/basins → spurious mixtures → signal+crosstalk From Hebbian cell assemblies to the binary Hopfield abstraction, distinguish the biological hypothesis, state variable, encoding rule, and retrieval dynamics. Execute asynchronous sign updates by hand, compute overlap, and explain how symmetric weights and a zero diagonal support energy descent. Derive the energy change from flipping one neuron and the local field for a \(P=1\) stored pattern, identifying aligned, antialigned, and spurious attractors. Separate a multi-pattern local field into signal and crosstalk, estimating variance, error probability, and loading \(\alpha =P/N\). Explain why \(\alpha c\approx 0.138\) applies only under the assumptions of the classic dense, unbiased, random Hopfield model, and compare sparse stochastic and global-inhibition variants. The Hopfield model abstracts explicit memory as attractor dynamics: recurrent updates drive a partial cue toward a stored pattern. Symmetric weights and asynchronous single-neuron updates ensure that Ising energy cannot increase. For \(P=1\), Hebbian weights make both the target and its sign-reversed pattern fixed points. For \(P>1\), the other memories produce crosstalk noise; as loading \(\alpha =P/N\) rises, retrieval errors increase, and stable retrieval disappears near \(\alpha \approx 0.138\) in the classic dense random model. Applying an energy proof for asynchronous dynamics to synchronous dynamics. Forgetting that W must be symmetric and \(W_{ii}=0\). Calling only \(\xi\) an attractor for \(P=1\) while overlooking \(-\xi\) and the spurious states implied by global sign symmetry. Conflating overlap with exact bit accuracy. Failing to check how crosstalk variance scales with N and P. Treating the Gaussian approximation as an exact finite-N law. Treating 0.138N as the memory capacity of the brain. Failing to state that a 'memory capacity of 0.138N' refers only to the stable-retrieval criterion of the classic dense random-pattern Hopfield model, not to a conclusion about biological memory capacity. binary neuron state \(S_{i} \in  {-1, +1}\) classic dense model asynchronous update \(S_{i} \leftarrow  \operatorname{sgn}(h_{i} )\) one neuron at a time Hopfield energy \(1\sum  E=- W_{ij} S_{i} S_{j} 2\) ij symmetric W Hebbian storage rule \(W_{ij} = N -1 \xi _{i} \xi _{j}\) µ \(W_{ii}=0\) pattern overlap mµ = N −1 \(\xi \) i Si \(i \pm 1\) patterns retrieval field decomposition h = signal + crosstalk random-pattern analysis loading ratio \(\alpha  = P /N P\) memories, N neurons classic capacity threshold \(\alpha c \approx  0.138\) dense unbiased random Hopfield associative memory The recovery of a stored pattern from a partial or noisy cue. cell assembly A group of neurons that are coactive and linked by Hebbian connections. basin of attraction The set of initial states that converge to the same attractor. pattern completion The reconstruction of a complete memory from an incomplete cue. asynchronous update An update scheme that changes only one unit at each step. Ising energy A Lyapunov function for a symmetric binary network. overlap The normalized dot product between the current state and a stored pattern. crosstalk Interference from other stored patterns during retrieval of a target pattern. spurious attractor A stable state that does not correspond to any single stored pattern. spin glass A regime dominated by many disordered metastable states. temperature A scale parameter for noise in stochastic updates. Why does \(m>0\) not guarantee successful retrieval? It measures only similarity at the start. The basin also depends on memory load, the particular crosstalk, update order, and network parameters. The Hebbian assembly hypothesis proposes that cells jointly active in an experience develop stronger mutual connections. Encoding changes the connections, a partial cue reactivates some members, and recurrent excitation recruits the missing members to complete the pattern. An engram is a cellular ensemble causally involved in memory storage and expression; activation correlation alone is insufficient for that label. Why does updating every neuron once not guarantee a fixed point? After an early unit is updated, later unit changes can alter its local field, so another complete sweep without changes is required. One sweep commonly means an average of N updates and does not imply convergence. Stop only after a full check finds no unit that would change or when both state and energy reach a fixed point. A finite deterministic asynchronous system under strict energy descent cannot visit new states forever, although arbitrary flipping on zero-field ties can create degeneracy. Why does the derivation of \(\Delta E\) fail when W is asymmetric? Pair terms with i as the first and second index cannot be combined into the same local field, so one scalar energy need not decline under updating. Nonincreasing energy guarantees arrival at some local minimum, not the global minimum or target memory. A noisy cue may cross a basin boundary and reach a spurious state. Symmetric W is central to the proof. Asymmetric plasticity or delays can generate cycles, chaos, or sequential dynamics, so the same Lyapunov function cannot still be used to claim convergence. Why does low mixture energy not make it a correct memory? Correctness is defined by the training target and behavioral identity; energy determines dynamical stability and does not know which patterns were designated as memories. Basin boundaries shrink as P increases. A cue can have its highest overlap with the target and still flow to a mixture because all stored patterns jointly shape the energy landscape. Any analogy to experimental 'memory blending' is only a hypothesis; real memory distortion also depends on semantic inference, overlap during encoding, and systems consolidation. Why does \(\alpha =0.1\) below 0.138 still not guarantee success for every cue? The threshold is a large-N typical statistic under a particular retrieval criterion. Finite patterns, poor cues, basin differences, and random instances can still fail. For independent unbiased patterns, one nontarget overlap \(\sum _j\xi _{j}^{\mu }\xi _{j}^{1}\) has \(\operatorname{mean} 0\) and variance approximately N. After multiplication by 1/N, one pattern contributes field variance of about 1/N. Summing P-1 nearly independent terms gives crosstalk variance \((P-1)/N\approx \alpha\). This motivates a Gaussian-noise approximation through the central limit theorem. Why does an uncentered 0/1 Hebbian rule produce a global positive bias? Only jointly active bits contribute positively, while inactivity supplies no canceling term. Across many patterns, most weights become positive and drive excessive activity. Place global inhibition directly in every weight by subtracting \(\gamma /(aN)\) after the centered Hebbian term. In the local field, this uniform negative term becomes \(-(\gamma /(aN))\sum _jS_{j}\), so a larger active population imposes stronger inhibition on every unit. Together with stochastic threshold u, it constrains total activity near aN. It is not one particular inhibitory neuron; rewriting it as an adaptive threshold requires an explicit mapping to population activity. Which interpretation is supported by the schematic “Hopfield basins: descent does not guarantee correct recall”? With symmetric weights, a zero diagonal, and asynchronous updates, both paths make E nonincreasing, but the cue's basin determines the endpoint. A cue near the target can complete to \(\xi ^{\mu }\), whereas crosstalk may draw an ambiguous cue into a mixture. Low energy therefore guarantees stability, not correct recall.

title: Lecture 27: Systems Consolidation and Generalization
subtitle: Systems Consolidation and Generalization
text: Systems Consolidation and Generalization Recent versus remote memory → hippocampal replay → Teacher–Student–Notebook → pattern separation and completion → memory error → generalization error Distinguish changes over time in memory's anatomical dependence from changes in its psychological character, and interpret patient E.P. and recent-versus-remote evidence cautiously. Define the Teacher, Student, and Notebook and their information flows one by one, separating environmental generation, one-shot storage, replay, and slow cortical learning. Explain how pattern separation, pattern completion, and Hebbian Student↔Notebook links support rapid encoding and replay from a partial cue. Calculate memory error and population generalization error by hand in a linear Teacher/Student model, and identify overfitting to noise. Use predictability and SNR to reason about the Go-CLS stopping condition and lesion predictions without presenting formal-model outputs as established biological facts. Systems consolidation changes both the anatomical dependence and the psychological character of memory: recent memories tend to be more vivid and episodic, whereas remote memories tend to be more gist-like and semantic. In the Teacher–Student–Notebook framework, the environment or Teacher is a generative source, the neocortical Student slowly learns predictive structure, and the hippocampal Notebook rapidly stores and replays one-shot episodes. Continuous standard transfer can also write unpredictable noise into the Student and thereby impair generalization. Go-CLS instead controls transfer according to signal predictability/SNR and stops at the optimum, so unpredictable episodic detail remains hippocampus-dependent. A single case such as patient E.P. cannot establish every mechanism of consolidation. Recent memory is not absolutely equivalent to hippocampal storage, nor is remote memory absolutely equivalent to neocortical storage. A correlation with replay does not by itself demonstrate causal synaptic transfer. Teacher, Student, and Notebook are formal roles rather than one-to-one anatomical labels. Memory error and generalization error are distinct metrics. Lower training error does not necessarily mean that consolidation is better. Go-CLS predictions are not established facts. Empirical observations, standard theory, the Teacher–Student–Notebook formal model, and Go-CLS predictions must be distinguished clearly, and model predictions must not be presented as established facts. Linear teacher model y = wTT \(x + \epsilon \) The target contains signal plus unpredictable noise. Student predictor ŷ = wST x The model is linear. Memory/training error em = P −1 (yµ − ŷµ )2 The patterns are stored. Population generalization error eg = \(E[(y - \hat{y})2 ]\) The experiences are new. Predictability/SNR λs = V ar(signal)/V ar(noise) The variances are finite. Optimal stopping t∗ = arg min eg (t) The learning curve is measurable. Consolidation channel replay → student updates This channel is a formal-model hypothesis. systems consolidation The time-dependent change in a memory's dependence on or representation across brain systems. episodic memory Memory for a particular event, including its time, place, and details. semantic memory Memory for abstract, generalized knowledge. replay The reactivation of experience-related neural sequences during rest or sleep. complementary learning systems, CLS A framework that combines fast hippocampal learning with slow cortical learning. Teacher-Student-Notebook A set of formal roles comprising a generative source, a slow predictor, and a one-shot associative memory. pattern separation A process that maps similar experiences onto more distinct memory codes. pattern completion A process that recovers a stored episode from a partial cue. memory error The reconstruction or prediction error measured on stored examples. generalization error The expected prediction error on new samples. overfitting The fitting of sample-specific noise that worsens performance on new data. generalization-optimized complementary learning systems, Go-CLS A model that controls consolidation according to generalization and predictability. Why does correct recall of facts from a remote memory not show that the original episode was preserved intact? Facts can be reconstructed from semantic knowledge, rehearsal, or schemas; spatiotemporal and perceptual details must be tested separately. The standard systems-consolidation account holds that recent memory initially depends on hippocampal indexing. Through replay and reactivation, neocortical connections gradually become able to support retrieval. Temporally graded amnesia, hippocampal lesions, and remote knowledge provide evidence. This is not the movement of a physical memory file from one place to another; it is a reorganization of network dependence. Why need Notebook replay not reproduce the original experience pixel for pixel? It can serve as a training sample as long as it reconstructs the task-relevant statistics or targets required for Student learning; the required fidelity is a modeling assumption. With only a slow Student, a rare experience may disappear before it is learned. With only a fast Notebook, episodes can be recalled accurately, but population regularities are difficult to extract and both capacity and interference remain limiting. Complementary timescales first write online experiences into the Notebook; later, interleaved replay mixes old and new samples for the Student and reduces the overwriting of old structure by new learning. Why is stronger pattern separation not always better? If similar partial cues are mapped with no continuity, retrieval addresses become fragile; stronger separation also consumes finite code space. Separation and completion operate at different stages: encoding increases distances among episodes, whereas retrieval decreases the distance between a cue and a stored pattern within one basin. Excessive separation can prevent a partial cue from generalizing to the right address; excessive completion can force an ambiguous cue into the wrong episode. The two processes must balance capacity, specificity, and robustness. Why can the minimum generalization error remain above zero? The Teacher target contains unpredictable noise \(\epsilon\). Even if the Student recovers the true weight, it cannot predict \(\epsilon\) in a new episode. Experiments must assess training memory and generalization on different stimuli. Testing on the same episodes used for training measures only memory error and cannot establish schema learning. P, input dimensionality, noise variance, and learning time should also be reported because they determine when overfitting occurs. Why does 'stopping consolidation' not mean deleting the Notebook memory? What stops is further Student fitting of that component; the Notebook can still preserve it and support retrieval of episodic detail. Go-CLS defines the goal of consolidation as generalization, not complete copying of Notebook contents. Use the signal-to-noise-style quantity \(\lambda =E[(w_{\mathrm{T}}^\mathrm{T} x)^{2}]/E[\epsilon ^{2}]\). It can be simplified to a variance ratio only when predictable signal and noise have both been centered. With high \(\lambda\), cross-episode regularity is strong and the Student benefits from replay for longer. With low \(\lambda\), sample-specific detail dominates, the generalization optimum occurs earlier, and transfer should stop or weaken. Which interpretation is supported by the schematic “The offline replay channel in Teacher–Student–Notebook”? During online learning, Teacher generates training experiences, and each Student pattern \(z^{\mu }\) is stored together with its Notebook code \(\xi ^{\mu }\). During retrieval, the Notebook first completes a partial cue and then uses V to compute \(\widetilde{z}_i=\sum _jV_{ij}\xi _{j}\). The dashed replay path returns the reconstructed activity to Student, allowing Student to continue learning while Teacher is absent.
